Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA): defined as aortic diameter >3 cm; risk of rupture rises sharply above 5.5 cm (men) and 5.0 cm (women).
Rupture presents as triad of hypotension, back/abdominal pain, and pulsatile abdominal mass — mortality without surgery >90%.
Symptomatic or rapidly expanding AAA (>1 cm/year or >0.5 cm/6 months) warrants urgent repair regardless of size.
A first episode of "renal colic" over 60 without a stone history is a leaking AAA until the aorta has been imaged (bedside ultrasound / CT angiography).
Suspected rupture: permissive hypotension (target systolic 70–90 mmHg while conscious) — no large crystalloid bolus; immediate vascular surgery (ESVS 2024).
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Immediate vascular surgery referral — emergency repair pathway (ESVS 2024)
• Permissive hypotension: avoid large fluid boluses while the patient is conscious; blood products via the major haemorrhage pathway (ESVS 2024)
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Herbal / Ayurvedic product history taken (heavy-metal risk).
• Urine ACR — hypertensive nephropathy screen.
• Document bilateral BP — coarctation exclusion if > 20mmHg differential.

management.text: - Beta-blocker (bisoprolol): tachycardia may be blunted — heart rate can under-read shock or sepsis (ATLS 10).

[immediate] If haemodynamically unstable: Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.
[immediate] Unstable fast AF: emergency synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation/anaesthesia (Resuscitation Council UK 2021).

[conservative] Stable: rate control first line — beta-blocker (e.g. bisoprolol) or rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker (diltiazem, verapamil); digoxin for sedentary patients or with heart failure (NICE NG196).
[conservative] Anticoagulation: assess CHA₂DS₂-VASc and bleeding risk; offer a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) when CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2 (consider ≥ 1 in men) — NICE NG196.
[conservative] Onset < 48 h and stable: rhythm control (electrical or pharmacological cardioversion) is an option with cardiology.
[followup] Cardiology / AF clinic; defer elective surgery until rate controlled and anticoagulation decided.

Investigation: Echocardiography (structural heart disease, LV function) (routine)

Diltiazem 60 mg PO (oral) TDS, titrate — Rate control — alternative (avoid with reduced LV function)

• Suggest aspirin loading dose 150–300 mg orally (ESC 2023) unless allergic, actively bleeding or otherwise contraindicated — clinician decision
• ST elevation / STEMI: immediate reperfusion — primary PCI pathway via cardiology (fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be delivered in time; ESC 2023)
• Oxygen only if SpO₂ < 90% (ESC 2023); IV access; continuous ECG monitoring during transfer

• Emergency synchronised DC cardioversion for haemodynamically unstable AF (ESC 2024) — resuscitation team
• IV loop diuretic (furosemide) for congestion (ESC 2021); sit upright; oxygen if SpO₂ < 90%
• No IV fluid bolus while heart-failure signs are present

• Assess with the 4AT; look for and treat the cause: sepsis / anastomotic leak, hypoxia, pain, urinary retention, constipation, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics), electrolytes, alcohol withdrawal (NICE CG103)
• No IV fluid bolus (heart-failure signs or suspected PE recorded — ESC 2021 HF; ESC 2019 PE); urgent echocardiography and senior review.
• POCUS: cardiac (effusion/tamponade), aorta (AAA — bedside ultrasound of the aorta), IVC collapsibility.
• Contact appropriate specialty immediately: cardiology (MI/tamponade), surgery (haemorrhage/AAA), emergency medicine (PE).
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
No routine coagulation test with standard DOAC interruption (PAUSE; ACCP 2022)

• apixaban: high-bleeding-risk procedure — omit for the interval set by drug and creatinine clearance (PAUSE; BSG/ESGE 2021). Low-risk endoscopy — omit the morning dose only. No LMWH bridging for a DOAC.

• No routine LMWH bridging for atrial fibrillation (BRIDGE trial; ACCP 2022); bridging only for high thrombotic risk (e.g. mechanical mitral valve, VTE in the last 3 months), decided with haematology.
• Supplemental O₂: titrate to SpO₂ 94–98% (BTS 2017); reassess.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• Heart-failure signs or suspected PE recorded: IV fluids withheld — BNP, echocardiography and diuretic review (ESC 2021; ESC 2019).

• Document bilateral BP — coarctation exclusion if > 20mmHg differential.

• DXA bone density scan — osteoporosis screening (USPSTF 2018, women ≥ 65).

Score action — qSOFA 3: 2 or more — qSOFA >= 2: high risk of a poor outcome. If suspected infection, treat as sepsis: lactate, blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 h, fluid resuscitation guided by perfusion and senior review (SSC 2021); otherwise look for another cause of organ dysfunction.

management.text: [immediate] Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.
[immediate] Remove the trigger; call for help; lie flat with legs raised (sit up if breathing is difficult).

[immediate] IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh: adult and child > 12 years 500 micrograms (0.5 mL); child 6–12 years 300 micrograms (0.3 mL); child 6 months–6 years 150 micrograms (0.15 mL); under 6 months 100–150 micrograms (RCUK 2021). Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement.
[immediate] High-flow oxygen; IV access; IV fluid bolus of crystalloid for circulatory compromise — adults 500–1000 mL, children 10 mL/kg (RCUK 2021).
[immediate] Refractory (no improvement after two IM doses): low-dose IV adrenaline infusion by critical care / anaesthetist (RCUK 2021 refractory algorithm).
[conservative] After stabilisation with IM adrenaline: a non-sedating oral antihistamine may help skin symptoms; corticosteroids are not routinely indicated (RCUK 2021).
[followup] Observe (≥ 6–12 h per RCUK risk assessment); discharge with two adrenaline auto-injectors and training, written plan, allergy clinic referral; record the allergy.

• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Meropenem 1g TDS + Vancomycin 25mg/kg (septic shock — broad cover).
• IV fluid resuscitation: 30ml/kg Hartmann's bolus — reassess lactate and BP at 30 min.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Vasopressors: Noradrenaline 0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min if MAP < 65 after 30ml/kg fluid.
• HDU/ICU admission — continuous BP monitoring, lactate trend.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• Supplemental O₂: titrate to SpO₂ 94–98% (BTS 2017); reassess.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.

management.text: [immediate] Outpatient clinic: obstetric emergency — call 911 or arrange immediate transfer to a hospital with an obstetric unit (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); inform the on-call obstetric team before arrival.
[immediate] Treat severe hypertension: labetalol (oral or IV) first line; nifedipine or IV hydralazine as alternatives — target BP ≤ 135/85 mmHg (NICE NG133).

[immediate] Eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia: magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 5–15 minutes, then 1 g/h for 24 h; further 2–4 g over 5–15 minutes for a recurrent seizure (Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen, NICE NG133). Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output.
[immediate] Eclamptic seizure: airway, left lateral position, oxygen; magnesium sulfate (not diazepam) first line.
[conservative] Severe pre-eclampsia: limit maintenance fluids to 80 mL/h unless there are ongoing losses (NICE NG133).
[surgical] Timing and mode of delivery by the obstetric team once the mother is stabilised (delivery is the definitive treatment).
[followup] Postpartum: continue antihypertensive treatment — choice with the obstetric team, compatible with breastfeeding (NICE NG133); pre-eclampsia can present up to 6 weeks after birth.

management.text: [immediate] Suspected PE with hypoxia, chest pain or collapse seen in clinic: Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.

[immediate] High-risk (massive) PE: IV unfractionated heparin (UFH) 80 units/kg bolus without delay, then systemic thrombolysis — alteplase 100 mg over 2 h (ESC 2019). Thrombolysis is contraindicated after major surgery, trauma or head injury in the previous 3 weeks, active bleeding, haemorrhagic stroke or recent ischaemic stroke — then surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy.
[conservative] Non-high-risk PE: anticoagulation with a DOAC (e.g. rivaroxaban 15 mg BD × 21 days then 20 mg OD, or apixaban) or LMWH; warfarin if a DOAC is contraindicated (NICE NG158).
[conservative] Low-risk PE (PESI I–II, normal troponin/BNP, adequate home support): early discharge protocol.
[followup] Duration of anticoagulation: 3 months for provoked, ≥6 months for unprovoked; reassess bleeding vs clot risk at 3 months.

Troponin and BNP predict right heart strain; PESI score guides outpatient vs inpatient management.

management.text: - Immunosuppressed (asplenia): fever, peritonism and a raised white cell count may be blunted — lower threshold for imaging, senior review and escalation.

[immediate] Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.

[immediate] Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour for high-risk sepsis per the local sepsis policy (NICE NG51); neutropenic sepsis — piperacillin-tazobactam within 1 hour (NICE CG151); asplenia — ceftriaxone without delay.
[immediate] Lactate > 2 mmol/L or SBP < 90 mmHg: IV crystalloid 500 mL over < 15 minutes and reassess; smaller aliquots with heart failure (NICE NG51).
[immediate] Oxygen to SpO₂ 94–98% (88–92% if at risk of hypercapnia); urine output monitoring; senior review and critical care if not improving.
[surgical] Source control (drainage, debridement, device removal) as early as feasible.
[followup] Review antibiotics at 48–72 h against cultures; asplenia — vaccination and prophylaxis review after recovery.

Asplenic patients (overwhelming post-splenectomy infection) and neutropenic patients deteriorate within hours.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV ceftriaxone without delay — do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture or imaging (NICE NG240)
• Suspected meningococcal disease with transfer delay: IM/IV benzylpenicillin before transfer unless penicillin anaphylaxis (NICE NG240)
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS — empirical sepsis cover.
• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Asplenia vaccinations per the current UKHSA Green Book ch. 7 schedule: pneumococcal, Hib/MenC, meningococcal ACWY (MenACWY) and meningococcal B (MenB), and annual influenza.
• Offer antibiotic prophylaxis and an emergency standby course (BSH 2011); splenectomy alert card; seek urgent assessment for any fever.
• Fever or skin / line-site infection — ask about IV drips: asked.
• Hepatitis B vaccination if serology shows no immunity (ACIP 2022).
• Diabetes screening (ADA 2024): HbA1c or fasting glucose; repeat every 3 years if normal, yearly if prediabetes.
• Calculate 10-year cardiovascular (ASCVD) risk — statin discussion if ≥ 10% with a risk factor (USPSTF 2022).

Score action — NEWS2 10: High — NEWS2 >= 7: continuous monitoring and an emergency response by a team with critical-care skills; consider HDU/ICU. In the clinic, call 911 for transfer to the nearest emergency department (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 2: 2 or more — qSOFA >= 2: high risk of a poor outcome. If suspected infection, treat as sepsis: lactate, blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 h, fluid resuscitation guided by perfusion and senior review (SSC 2021); otherwise look for another cause of organ dysfunction.

management.text: [immediate] Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.
[immediate] While waiting: two large-bore cannulae, bloods and crossmatch; alert the on-call vascular surgery team at the receiving hospital.
[conservative] Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics after blood cultures, per microbiology advice; prolonged antimicrobial therapy after graft infection (ESVS 2020).
[surgical] Vascular surgery: graft excision with in situ reconstruction or extra-anatomic bypass and repair of the bowel; endovascular stent-graft as a bridge in the unstable patient (ESVS 2020).
[followup] Lifelong vascular surveillance; long-term antimicrobial therapy as the vascular and infection teams advise (ESVS 2020).

Any gastrointestinal bleeding in a patient with an aortic graft (open repair or EVAR) is a secondary aorto-enteric fistula until proven otherwise; a self-limiting "herald" bleed often precedes exsanguinating haemorrhage (ESVS 2020).
CT angiography is the first test; endoscopy must not delay it, and a normal endoscopy does not exclude a fistula (ESVS 2020).

PRE-OPERATIVE:
• NBM — emergency case, starved status documented.
• IV Pip-Tazo 4.5g + Metronidazole 500mg at induction.
• LMWH + TED stockings (DVT prophylaxis).
• Consent obtained (emergency consent if incapacitated): perforation risk, conversion to open, wound infection, right-sided port-sit …(truncated)

• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.

[followup] Secondary prevention (dual antiplatelet therapy, statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor as indicated) and cardiac rehabilitation per cardiology; defer elective surgery (ESC/ESAIC 2022).

Atypical presentations are common in women, older people and people with diabetes: epigastric pain, breathlessness, nausea or "indigestion" — record a 12-lead ECG in every adult with unexplained upper abdominal or chest pain.
Inferior STEMI often presents as epigastric pain with vomiting and is mislabelled biliary colic or gastritis.
In pregnancy, spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a leading cause of ACS.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Suggest aspirin loading dose 150–300 mg orally (ESC 2023) unless allergic, actively bleeding or otherwise contraindicated — clinician decision
• ST elevation / STEMI: immediate reperfusion — primary PCI pathway via cardiology (fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be delivered in time; ESC 2023)
• Oxygen only if SpO₂ < 90% (ESC 2023); IV access; continuous ECG monitoring during transfer
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ketones — exclude diabetic ketoacidosis.
• Variable-rate insulin infusion (VRIII) if inpatient glucose consistently > 11 mmol/L.
• Diabetology review — adjust long-term insulin/OHG regimen.
• Urine albumin:creatinine ratio — diabetic nephropathy screening.
• Urine ACR — hypertensive nephropathy screen.
• Document bilateral BP — coarctation exclusion if > 20mmHg differential.

• Pregnancy: inform the obstetric / maternity team — joint care.
• Fetal monitoring (CTG / fetal heart rate) with the obstetric team.

• Pregnancy-safe plan: no NSAIDs from 20 weeks (MHRA 2020); anticoagulation with LMWH — DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated in pregnancy (warfarin is teratogenic) (RCOG GTG 37a/b); ultrasound or MRI before ionising imaging where it answers the question.
• Consider MRI breast if dense glandular tissue or BRCA status.
• Refer breast oncology — 2-week wait pathway if clinically suspicious.
• Document family history of breast/ovarian cancer — BRCA risk assessment.

• Document date and result of last cervical screening test.
• Cervical screening: primary HPV test every 5 years (USPSTF 2018 / WHO 2021); cytology every 3 years if HPV testing unavailable.
• Hepatitis B vaccination if serology shows no immunity (ACIP 2022).

LAPAROSCOPIC CHOLECYSTECTOMY — OPERATIVE PLAN
─────────────────────────────────────────────
PRE-OPERATIVE:
• Fasting: food up to 6 h and clear fluids up to 2 h before anaesthesia (AAGBI 2010; ESA 2011).
• Antibiotic prophylaxis: single dose at induction per the local antimicrobial policy (SIGN 104 high-risk laparoscopic cholecystectomy); check the allergy record.
• VTE prophylaxis pe …(truncated)
• USS abdomen — biliary tree, gallstones, hepatic parenchyma.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS — empirical sepsis cover.
• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• VTE risk assessment on admission (NICE NG89).
• Mechanical prophylaxis: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression unless contraindicated (NICE NG89).
• Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH unless bleeding risk outweighs it (dose adjusted for renal function); extended to 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery (NICE NG89).

Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) grade severity: Grade I mild, II moderate, III severe with organ dysfunction.

Grade I–II: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 h of admission, up to 7 days of symptoms) if fit (CCI/ASA-PS); Grade III: early surgery only in a favourable patient at an advanced centre, otherwise gallbladder drainage and delayed cholecystectomy when stable (TG18).

• IV Co-amoxiclav 1.2g TDS if systemic inflammatory criteria met.
• NBM, IV Hartmann's, regular analgesia (paracetamol + morphine PRN).
• Plan laparoscopic cholecystectomy — early (< 72h onset) or interval (≥ 6 weeks).
• Obtain surgical consent — laparoscopic cholecystectomy risks/alternatives.
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Ketones urgently — blood ketones > 3 mmol/L = DKA; urine ketones > 2+ = DKA screen positive.

• If DKA (ketones ≥ 3 mmol/L + pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 15): fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h with potassium replacement (JBDS 2023). If HHS (osmolality ≥ 320, ketones < 3): IV 0.9% sodium chloride first; fixed-rate insulin 0.05 units/kg/h only once glucose stops falling with fluids (JBDS 2022). Monitor K⁺ hourly.
• Defer elective surgery — target glucose 6–10 mmol/L, ketones < 0.5 mmol/L pre-operatively.
• USS RUQ — gallbladder wall thickness (> 4mm), pericholecystic fluid, stones, CBD diameter.
• Consent: laparoscopic cholecystectomy — bile duct injury (0.3%), haemorrhage, conversion to open, bile leak, retained stone, wound infection.

LAPAROSCOPIC CHOLECYSTECTOMY — OPERATIVE PLAN
─────────────────────────────────────────────
PRE-OPERATIVE:
• Fasting: food up to 6 h and clear fluids up to 2 h before anaesthesia (AAGBI 2010; ESA 2011).
• Antibiotic prophylaxis: single dose at induction per the local antimicrobial policy (SIGN 104 high-risk laparoscopic cholecystectomy); check the allergy record.
• VTE prophylaxis (N …(truncated)
• USS RUQ — confirm cholecystitis (wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid).
• IV Co-amoxiclav 1.2g TDS if systemic inflammatory criteria met.
• NBM, IV Hartmann's, regular analgesia (paracetamol + morphine PRN).
• Plan laparoscopic cholecystectomy — early (< 72h onset) or interval (≥ 6 weeks).
• Obtain surgical consent — laparoscopic cholecystectomy risks/alternatives.
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS — empirical sepsis cover.
• No IV fluid bolus: heart-failure signs or suspected PE recorded — senior review of fluid strategy (ESC 2021; ESC 2019).
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• Controlled oxygen via Venturi mask (24–28%), target SpO₂ 88–92% (BTS 2017 — COPD / hypercapnic risk); arterial blood gas within 1 hour; NIV if pH < 7.35 with raised PaCO₂.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• VTE risk assessment on admission (NICE NG89).
• Mechanical prophylaxis: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression unless contraindicated (NICE NG89).
• Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH unless bleeding risk outweighs it (dose adjusted for renal function); extended to 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery (NICE NG89).

Grade I–II: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 h of admission, up to 7 days of symptoms) if fit (CCI/ASA-PS); Grade III: early surgery only in a favourable patient at an advanced centre, otherwise gallbladder drainage and delayed cholecystectomy when stable (TG18).

management.text: [immediate] High severity (CURB-65 ≥ 3, sepsis, hypoxia) seen in clinic: Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.
[immediate] Oxygen to SpO₂ 94–98% (88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, e.g. COPD — BTS 2017).

[immediate] Moderate severity: amoxicillin, adding clarithromycin if atypical pathogens are suspected; high severity: IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g three times daily plus clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily — review at 48 h, total 5 days (NICE NG138).
[conservative] Low severity (CURB-65 0–1): oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days (NICE NG138).
[conservative] Immunosuppressed host: discuss early with respiratory/microbiology — consider Pneumocystis (PCP), methotrexate pneumonitis, TB and resistant organisms.
[followup] Review at 48–72 h; repeat CXR at 6 weeks if symptoms persist or high cancer risk (smoker > 50).

Lower-lobe pneumonia commonly presents as upper abdominal pain (right lower lobe mimics cholecystitis or appendicitis, especially in children) — CXR before abdominal surgery.
CURB-65 (CRB-65 in the community) grades severity and guides antibiotic choice and admission.
Immunosuppressed patients: consider Pneumocystis (PCP), drug-induced pneumonitis (e.g. methotrexate) and TB.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh — adult / child > 12 years (RCUK 2021); repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement
• Remove the trigger; lie flat with legs raised (sit up if breathing is difficult); high-flow oxygen
• IV fluid bolus 500–1000 mL crystalloid if shocked (RCUK 2021)
• Record the allergy; do not re-expose; refer to allergy clinic and issue adrenaline auto-injector training on discharge (RCUK 2021)
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• ATLS primary survey; do not remove an impaled object; cover eviscerated bowel with moist dressings; trauma surgery
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS — empirical sepsis cover.
• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• Supplemental O₂: titrate to SpO₂ 94–98% (BTS 2017); reassess.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Fever or skin / line-site infection — ask about IV drips: asked.

Score action — NEWS2 9: High — NEWS2 >= 7: continuous monitoring and an emergency response by a team with critical-care skills; consider HDU/ICU. In the clinic, call 911 for transfer to the nearest emergency department (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 1: Below 2 — qSOFA < 2 does not exclude sepsis: continue NEWS2 monitoring and reassess if infection is suspected (Sepsis-3; SSC 2021 advises against qSOFA alone as a screening tool).

LAPAROSCOPIC CHOLECYSTECTOMY — OPERATIVE PLAN
─────────────────────────────────────────────
PRE-OPERATIVE:
• Fasting: food up to 6 h and clear fluids up to 2 h before anaesthesia (AAGBI 2010; ESA 2011).
• Antibiotic prophylaxis: single dose at induction per the local antimicrobial policy (SIGN 104 high-risk laparoscopic cholecystectomy); check the allergy record.
• VTE prophylaxis pe …(truncated)
• USS RUQ — confirm cholecystitis (wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid).
• IV Co-amoxiclav 1.2g TDS if systemic inflammatory criteria met.
• NBM, IV Hartmann's, regular analgesia (paracetamol + morphine PRN).
• Plan laparoscopic cholecystectomy — early (< 72h onset) or interval (≥ 6 weeks).
• Obtain surgical consent — laparoscopic cholecystectomy risks/alternatives.
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS — empirical sepsis cover.
• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• VTE risk assessment on admission (NICE NG89).
• Mechanical prophylaxis: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression unless contraindicated (NICE NG89).
• Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH unless bleeding risk outweighs it (dose adjusted for renal function); extended to 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery (NICE NG89).

management.text: Severe Cholecystitis — Tokyo Grade III — Source Control First
ICU-level resuscitation (sepsis-6 protocol). Percutaneous cholecystostomy (IR referral) for biliary decompression.
Delayed laparoscopic cholecystectomy when organ dysfunction resolved and patient fit.
- ⚠ Allergy cross-check: 3 item(s) withheld (penicillin allergy: Penicillin (Anaphylaxis)) — see the alternatives in the plan.
- Penicillin allergy recorded: check the reaction type — after an immediate (anaphylactic) penicillin reaction avoid cephalosporins and carbapenems unless there is no alternative (BNF).

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)
- Low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention: usually continue through surgery unless the bleeding risk is prohibitive (e.g. intracranial, spinal) — ESC/ESAIC 2022.
[immediate] NBM, IV analgesia (morphine + antiemetic), IV fluids.

[immediate] ⚠ ALLERGY — penicillin allergy recorded (Penicillin (Anaphylaxis)): withheld (contains co-amoxiclav, piperacillin-tazobactam). Alternative: Penicillin allergy (intra-abdominal infection, IDSA/SIS 2010; SIS 2017): ciprofloxacin + metronidazole, or gentamicin + metronidazole; a cephalosporin + metronidazole only if the reaction was not immediate/anaphylactic — doses per BNF …(truncated)
[surgical] Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 h for Grade I–II if fit (low CCI / ASA-PS — TG18).
[surgical] Gallbladder drainage (percutaneous cholecystostomy / PTGBD) for Grade III, or Grade II unfit for surgery (high CCI / ASA-PS) — TG18.
[surgical] Delayed cholecystectomy 6–8 weeks after drainage or recovery if the patient was unfit for early surgery.
[followup] Ensure histology of gallbladder specimen reviewed.

Murphy's sign has sensitivity 65% and specificity 87% for acute cholecystitis.
Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) grade severity: Grade I mild, II moderate, III severe with organ dysfunction.

Grade I–II: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 h of admission, up to 7 days of symptoms) if fit (CCI/ASA-PS); Grade III: early surgery only in a favourable patient at an advanced centre, otherwise gallbladder drainage and delayed cholecystectomy when stable (TG18).

• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Act on the critical result now: senior review, repeat and identify the cause
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Meropenem 1g TDS + Vancomycin 25mg/kg (septic shock — broad cover).
• IV fluid resuscitation: 30ml/kg Hartmann's bolus — reassess lactate and BP at 30 min.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Vasopressors: Noradrenaline 0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min if MAP < 65 after 30ml/kg fluid.
• HDU/ICU admission — continuous BP monitoring, lactate trend.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• USS RUQ — gallbladder wall thickness (> 4mm), pericholecystic fluid, stones, CBD diameter.
• Consent: laparoscopic cholecystectomy — bile duct injury (0.3%), haemorrhage, conversion to open, bile leak, retained stone, wound infection.

LAPAROSCOPIC CHOLECYSTECTOMY — OPERATIVE PLAN
─────────────────────────────────────────────
PRE-OPERATIVE:
• Fasting: food up to 6 h and clear fluids up to 2 h before anaesthesia (AAGBI 2010; ESA 2011).
• Antibiotic prophylaxis: single dose at induction per the local antimicrobial policy (SIGN 104 high-risk laparoscopic cholecystectomy); check the allergy record.
• VTE prophylaxis pe …(truncated)
• USS RUQ — confirm cholecystitis (wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid).

• ⚠ PENICILLIN ALLERGY recorded — the penicillin-class antibiotic proposed here is withheld: use a non-penicillin alternative per the local antimicrobial guideline (after anaphylaxis, avoid cephalosporins and carbapenems too unless allergy advice says otherwise).
• NBM, IV Hartmann's, regular analgesia (paracetamol + morphine PRN).
• Plan laparoscopic cholecystectomy — early (< 72h onset) or interval (≥ 6 weeks).
• Obtain surgical consent — laparoscopic cholecystectomy risks/alternatives.
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• Supplemental O₂: titrate to SpO₂ 94–98% (BTS 2017); reassess.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• Urine protein:creatinine ratio — nephrotic syndrome (PCR > 300mg/mmol).
• Dietitian referral — pre-operative nutritional support. Delay elective surgery ≥ 4 weeks if possible.
• Prescribe ONS (Ensure/Fortisip) ×2 — pre-op nutritional optimisation (ERAS).
• If albumin < 25 g/L and surgery urgent: parenteral nutrition pre-operatively with nutrition team support.
• VTE risk assessment on admission (NICE NG89).
• Mechanical prophylaxis: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression unless contraindicated (NICE NG89).
• Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH unless bleeding risk outweighs it (dose adjusted for renal function); extended to 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery (NICE NG89).
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ACR — hypertensive nephropathy screen.
• Document bilateral BP — coarctation exclusion if > 20mmHg differential.
• Fever or skin / line-site infection — ask about IV drips: asked.

Result action — Lactate 4.6 mmol/L: Lactate >= 4 mmol/L — Tissue hypoperfusion: find the cause (sepsis, bleeding, ischaemia, obstructive shock), resuscitate guided by perfusion, repeat lactate within 2-4 h, senior review and critical-care referral. If suspected infection, sepsis bundle now: blood cultures and IV antibiotics within 1 h (SSC 2021).

Score action — TG18 cholecystitis 3: Grade III (severe) — Grade III: organ support and antibiotics; urgent or early gallbladder drainage, unless the organ dysfunction is favourable and the patient is fit for early cholecystectomy in an advanced centre (TG18).

Score action — NEWS2 15: High — NEWS2 >= 7: continuous monitoring and an emergency response by a team with critical-care skills; consider HDU/ICU. In the clinic, call 911 for transfer to the nearest emergency department (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 3: 2 or more — qSOFA >= 2: high risk of a poor outcome. If suspected infection, treat as sepsis: lactate, blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 h, fluid resuscitation guided by perfusion and senior review (SSC 2021); otherwise look for another cause of organ dysfunction.

management.text: - VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Active bleeding / high bleeding risk: mechanical prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression) now; start LMWH once haemostasis is secure — reassess daily. Major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery: extend pharmacological prophylaxis to 28 days after surgery.
- Metformin: continue if only one meal is missed; omit if more than one meal will be missed, eGFR < 60 mL/min or IV contrast is planned (CPOC 2021).

[surgical] Colon cancer: laparoscopic or open resection by tumour site with D3 lymphadenectomy — right (or extended right) hemicolectomy for right-sided tumours; left hemicolectomy or sigmoid colectomy if left-sided.
[surgical] Obstructing right-sided or transverse cancer: right (or extended right) hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis in most patients (WSES 2018).

[surgical] Obstructing left-sided cancer: resection with anastomosis ± defunctioning stoma, Hartmann's procedure, or a colonic stent (SEMS) as a bridge — stenting is contraindicated with perforation, impending caecal perforation (tender caecum, ischaemia) or peritonitis (WSES 2018; ESGE 2020).
[surgical] Rectal cancer: anterior resection (or APR for low tumours); TEMS / TEM for T1 disease.
[conservative] Iron-deficiency anaemia before surgery: iron replacement (IV iron if surgery is within weeks) — BSG 2021.
[conservative] Older or frail patients: comprehensive geriatric assessment, delirium risk and prevention, and shared decision-making on goals of care before major surgery (CPOC 2021).
[conservative] Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for T3/T4 or N+ rectal cancers before surgery.
[conservative] Adjuvant chemotherapy (CAPOX or FOLFOX) for Stage III colon cancer.
[followup] Surveillance colonoscopy at 1 year, then 3-yearly; CEA + CT at 6-monthly intervals × 3 years.

Active bleeding / high bleeding risk: mechanical prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression) now; start LMWH once haemostasis is secure — reassess daily. Major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery: extend pharmacological prophylaxis to 28 days after surgery.

[surgical] Colon cancer: laparoscopic or open resection by tumour site with D3 lymphadenectomy — right (or extended right) hemicolectomy for right-sided tumours; left hemicolectomy or sigmoid colectomy if left-sided.
[surgical] Obstructing right-sided or transverse cancer: right (or extended right) hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis in most patients (WSES 2018).

[surgical] Obstructing left-sided cancer: resection with anastomosis ± defunctioning stoma, Hartmann's procedure, or a colonic stent (SEMS) as a bridge — stenting is contraindicated with perforation, impending caecal perforation (tender caecum, ischaemia) or peritonitis (WSES 2018; ESGE 2020).
[surgical] Rectal cancer: anterior resection (or APR for low tumours); TEMS / TEM for T1 disease.
[conservative] Iron-deficiency anaemia before surgery: iron replacement (IV iron if surgery is within weeks) — BSG 2021.
[conservative] Older or frail patients: comprehensive geriatric assessment, delirium risk and prevention, and shared decision-making on goals of care before major surgery (CPOC 2021).
[conservative] Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for T3/T4 or N+ rectal cancers before surgery.
[conservative] Adjuvant chemotherapy (CAPOX or FOLFOX) for Stage III colon cancer.

expectations.note: USPSTF 2021 / ACG 2021: average-risk screening from 45. ACG 2021: one FDR with CRC diagnosed < 60 (father at 58) → colonoscopy from age 40 (or 10 years before the relative’s age at diagnosis), repeated every 5 years — so he is overdue on the ACG reading. BSG 2020 (UK) would not add colonoscopic surveillance for a single FDR diagnosed ≥ 50. The practice’s policy needs the surgeon’s decision. Not observable in the web harness: the dashboard feeds the Family History field (ClinicalPromptsStrip familyHistory) to computeClinicalPrompts, but the vignette schema has no family-history input, so web-runner passes []. In the dashboard the "FHx colorectal cancer, age 35–49" prompt would probably add a colonoscopy. Needs a familyHistory input in the schema and both runners. Without a family history there is no screening prompt before 50: the average-risk "colorectal_screen" prompt starts at age 50 (USPSTF 2021 and ACG 2021: 45) and offers FOBT every 2 years rather than annual FIT. Web, 2026-09-25 (fix-web-screening): now observed in the harness — the preventive-screening engine reads the "Family history: …" and "Lynch syndrome" comorbidity entries, which the dashboard passes too; web removed from unverified.

management.text: Uncomplicated Acute Diverticulitis (NICE NG147 2019)

Antibiotics only if systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or with significant comorbidity: co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS for 5 days (penicillin allergy: cefalexin + metronidazole, trimethoprim + metronidazole, or ciprofloxacin + metronidazole — NICE NG147).

management.text: [immediate] Suspected PE with hypoxia, chest pain or collapse seen in clinic: Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.

[immediate] Oxygen to SpO₂ 94–98%; IV access; haemodynamic monitoring; alert anaesthetics/ICU if unstable. Avoid large fluid boluses — at most a cautious 500 mL challenge; noradrenaline for hypotension (ESC 2019).

[immediate] High-risk (massive) PE: IV unfractionated heparin (UFH) 80 units/kg bolus without delay, then systemic thrombolysis — alteplase 100 mg over 2 h (ESC 2019). Thrombolysis is contraindicated after major surgery, trauma or head injury in the previous 3 weeks, active bleeding, haemorrhagic stroke or recent ischaemic stroke — then surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy.
[conservative] Non-high-risk PE: anticoagulation with a DOAC (e.g. rivaroxaban 15 mg BD × 21 days then 20 mg OD, or apixaban) or LMWH; warfarin if a DOAC is contraindicated (NICE NG158).
[conservative] Low-risk PE (PESI I–II, normal troponin/BNP, adequate home support): early discharge protocol.
[followup] Duration of anticoagulation: 3 months for provoked, ≥6 months for unprovoked; reassess bleeding vs clot risk at 3 months.
[followup] Thrombophilia screen and malignancy workup if unprovoked; CTPA at 3–6 months to exclude chronic thromboembolic disease.

[immediate] Irreducible, tender hernia: nil by mouth, IV fluids and analgesia; assess for strangulation (skin changes, peritonism, systemic toxicity, raised lactate) — WSES 2017.

[conservative] Incarcerated without any sign of strangulation: a single gentle reduction by an experienced surgeon with analgesia may be considered; do not attempt reduction if strangulation is suspected (WSES 2017). If reduced, admit and repair on the same admission.

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)
- Low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention: usually continue through surgery unless the bleeding risk is prohibitive (e.g. intracranial, spinal) — ESC/ESAIC 2022.

• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Emergency surgical exploration and debridement; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; a low LRINEC score does not exclude NSTI (WSES 2018)
• Look for sepsis, hypoperfusion or ischaemia (e.g. mesenteric); repeat lactate
• Ketones urgently — blood ketones > 3 mmol/L = DKA; urine ketones > 2+ = DKA screen positive.

• If DKA (ketones ≥ 3 mmol/L + pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 15): fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h with potassium replacement (JBDS 2023). If HHS (osmolality ≥ 320, ketones < 3): IV 0.9% sodium chloride first; fixed-rate insulin 0.05 units/kg/h only once glucose stops falling with fluids (JBDS 2022). Monitor K⁺ hourly.
• Defer elective surgery — target glucose 6–10 mmol/L, ketones < 0.5 mmol/L pre-operatively.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS — empirical sepsis cover.
• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.

management.text: Uncomplicated Acute Diverticulitis (NICE NG147 2019)

Systemically well, immunocompetent: antibiotics not routinely needed — paracetamol (avoid NSAIDs and, where possible, opioids), clear fluids then diet as tolerated, safety-net advice, review within 48 h or sooner if worse.

Antibiotics only if systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or with significant comorbidity: co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS for 5 days (penicillin allergy: cefalexin + metronidazole, trimethoprim + metronidazole, or ciprofloxacin + metronidazole — NICE NG147).
Colonic evaluation (colonoscopy or CT colonography) after resolution if not recently done, to exclude colorectal cancer.

management.text: • Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV 0.9% sodium chloride fluid resuscitation (JBDS 2023)
• Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/h (JBDS 2023); continue long-acting basal insulin
• Potassium replacement in the IV fluids guided by hourly/2-hourly K⁺ (JBDS 2023)
• Add 10% glucose when blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L — and from the start in euglycaemic DKA (JBDS 2023)
• Pregnancy: joint obstetric and medical care; fetal monitoring (CTG)
• Abdominal pain may be caused by DKA — re-examine as the acidosis corrects before any operation
• Pregnancy: inform the obstetric / maternity team — joint care.
• Fetal monitoring (CTG / fetal heart rate) with the obstetric team.

• Pregnancy-safe plan: no NSAIDs from 20 weeks (MHRA 2020); anticoagulation with LMWH — DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated in pregnancy (warfarin is teratogenic) (RCOG GTG 37a/b); ultrasound or MRI before ionising imaging where it answers the question.
• Type 1 diabetes: continue long-acting basal insulin throughout (never omit — DKA risk); variable-rate IV insulin infusion if more than one meal will be missed (CPOC 2021).
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• IV fluid challenge 500ml if hypovolaemia likely — reassess HR at 30 min.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ketones — exclude diabetic ketoacidosis.
• Variable-rate insulin infusion (VRIII) if inpatient glucose consistently > 11 mmol/L.
• Diabetology review — adjust long-term insulin/OHG regimen.
• Urine albumin:creatinine ratio — diabetic nephropathy screening.
• Low potassium or sodium, dehydration or chronic constipation — ask about detox teas and cleanses: asked.

management.text: - β-HCG: result required before surgery, ionising imaging or a drug that is unsafe in pregnancy — do not record it as negative without a result.

[immediate] Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.
[immediate] Adults: IV 0.9% sodium chloride — 1 L over the first hour (500 mL over 10–15 min if SBP < 90 mmHg), then per the JBDS fluid schedule, adjusted for age, heart failure and renal failure.
[immediate] Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (FRIII) 0.1 units/kg/h (JBDS 2023).
[immediate] Continue long-acting (basal) insulin at the usual dose throughout (JBDS 2023).
[immediate] Potassium replacement in each litre of fluid by serum K⁺: > 5.5 mmol/L none; 3.5–5.5 mmol/L potassium chloride 40 mmol/L; < 3.5 mmol/L senior review for additional potassium (JBDS 2023).
[immediate] Add 10% glucose at 125 mL/h alongside the saline when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L — from the start in euglycaemic DKA (JBDS 2023).
[immediate] Stop any SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin); do not restart without specialist review (MHRA).
[conservative] Targets: ketones fall ≥ 0.5 mmol/L/h, bicarbonate rise ≥ 3 mmol/L/h, glucose fall 3 mmol/L/h; VTE prophylaxis; treat the precipitant; diabetes team review.

DKA = ketonaemia ≥ 3 mmol/L (or ketonuria 2+) with bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L and/or venous pH < 7.3; glucose may be NORMAL with SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycaemic DKA).
Abdominal pain and vomiting are common in DKA — do not operate for DKA pain; treat DKA and reassess.
Children: cerebral oedema risk — BSPED protocol, hourly neurological observations.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV 0.9% sodium chloride fluid resuscitation (JBDS 2023)
• Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/h (JBDS 2023); continue long-acting basal insulin
• Potassium replacement in the IV fluids guided by hourly/2-hourly K⁺ (JBDS 2023)
• Add 10% glucose when blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L — and from the start in euglycaemic DKA (JBDS 2023)
• Abdominal pain may be caused by DKA — re-examine as the acidosis corrects before any operation
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Act on the critical result now: senior review, repeat and identify the cause
• If urine β-HCG positive: serum quantitative β-HCG + urgent TVS — exclude ectopic.
• If ectopic suspected: emergency gynaecology referral — surgical or medical management.
• Type 1 diabetes: continue long-acting basal insulin throughout (never omit — DKA risk); variable-rate IV insulin infusion if more than one meal will be missed (CPOC 2021).
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• IV fluid challenge 500ml if hypovolaemia likely — reassess HR at 30 min.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ketones — exclude diabetic ketoacidosis.
• Variable-rate insulin infusion (VRIII) if inpatient glucose consistently > 11 mmol/L.
• Diabetology review — adjust long-term insulin/OHG regimen.
• Urine albumin:creatinine ratio — diabetic nephropathy screening.
• Low potassium or sodium, dehydration or chronic constipation — ask about detox teas and cleanses: asked.
Score action — NEWS2 6: Medium (key threshold) — NEWS2 5-6: minimum hourly observations; urgent response by a clinician competent in acute illness; consider sepsis (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 1: Below 2 — qSOFA < 2 does not exclude sepsis: continue NEWS2 monitoring and reassess if infection is suspected (Sepsis-3; SSC 2021 advises against qSOFA alone as a screening tool).

[immediate] Same-day emergency surgical admission: nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia, NG tube if obstructed; correct electrolytes.

[conservative] Only if strangulation is not suspected: a single gentle reduction with analgesia by an experienced surgeon may be considered; if it reduces, admit, observe for peritonitis and repair semi-electively (WSES 2017).

[surgical] Strangulation suspected, or reduction fails: emergency repair (open or laparoscopic); assess bowel viability and resect non-viable bowel; mesh in a clean or clean-contaminated field, suture or biological repair if grossly contaminated (WSES 2017).
[followup] Wound review; smoking cessation and weight optimisation to lower recurrence risk.
Incarcerated = irreducible; strangulated = compromised blood supply. Skin change, peritonism, fever, tachycardia, raised lactate or WCC and CT findings suggest strangulation (WSES 2017).
Do not attempt reduction when strangulation is suspected — emergency repair.
Mesh repair is safe in clean and clean-contaminated fields; with gross contamination use a suture or biological repair (WSES 2017).

[immediate] Analgesia: an NSAID (e.g. diclofenac 75 mg IM / PR) first-line only if renal function is normal — NSAIDs contraindicated in AKI, eGFR < 30, an obstructed solitary kidney, pregnancy, active GI bleeding or significant bleeding risk; otherwise IV paracetamol ± opioid; antiemetic (EAU 2024; NICE NG118).

[immediate] Obstructed and infected kidney (fever, sepsis), anuria, bilateral obstruction or an obstructed solitary kidney: urgent decompression — percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric (JJ) stent — with IV antibiotics if infected; definitive stone treatment later (EAU 2024).

[conservative] MET (medical expulsive therapy): tamsulosin 0.4 mg OD for a distal ureteric stone > 5 mm and ≤ 10 mm for up to 4 weeks — not with infection, anuria, AKI or an obstructed solitary kidney, where decompression comes first (EAU 2024).
[conservative] High fluid intake (>2 L/day) — dilutes urine, prevents crystal aggregation.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA): defined as aortic diameter >3 cm; risk of rupture rises sharply above 5.5 cm (men) and 5.0 cm (women).
Rupture presents as triad of hypotension, back/abdominal pain, and pulsatile abdominal mass — mortality without surgery >90%.
Symptomatic or rapidly expanding AAA (>1 cm/year or >0.5 cm/6 months) warrants urgent repair regardless of size.
A first episode of "renal colic" over 60 without a stone history is a leaking AAA until the aorta has been imaged (bedside ultrasound / CT angiography).
Suspected rupture: permissive hypotension (target systolic 70–90 mmHg while conscious) — no large crystalloid bolus; immediate vascular surgery (ESVS 2024).

Most ovarian cysts in premenopausal women are functional (follicular, corpus luteum) and resolve within 2–3 menstrual cycles.
RMI (Risk of Malignancy Index) = ultrasound score × menopausal status × CA-125; RMI >200 warrants oncology review.
IOTA simple rules on ultrasound guide benign vs malignant classification for pre-operative assessment.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Urgent gynaecology review — ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency (diagnostic laparoscopy); ultrasound must not delay surgery
• If urine β-HCG positive: serum quantitative β-HCG + urgent TVS — exclude ectopic.
• If ectopic suspected: emergency gynaecology referral — surgical or medical management.
• Withhold the apixaban now (active bleeding).
• Anticoagulant reversal with haematology (ACC 2020 ECDP): andexanet alfa or four-factor PCC for major / life-threatening bleeding.
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• IV fluid challenge 500ml if hypovolaemia likely — reassess HR at 30 min.

management.text: EMERGENCY — Strangulated Hernia
Emergency laparoscopic/open hernia repair. Assess bowel viability — resect if necrotic (primary anastomosis vs stoma based on contamination).
Do NOT delay for imaging if clinical peritonism is present.

- apixaban and surgery (PAUSE 2019): omit 1 day before a low-bleed-risk and 2 days before a high-bleed-risk operation (check renal function); resume 1 day after low-risk and 2–3 days after high-risk surgery. No bridging, no routine pre-operative coagulation test (ACCP 2022).

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. On therapeutic anticoagulation: see the anticoagulation plan; while it is interrupted after surgery use mechanical prophylaxis and prophylactic-dose LMWH when bleeding risk allows.

- Frailty / delirium risk (age 82, age 82): delirium prevention and 4AT screening (NICE CG103); comprehensive geriatric assessment and elderly-medicine (geriatric) input; shared decision-making with goals of care and a treatment-escalation plan documented (CPOC 2021 perioperative care for people living with frailty).
[surgical] Elective: mesh plug repair (Lockwood) or laparoscopic TEP.
[surgical] Emergency: McEvedy approach (high inguinal) for access and bowel inspection.

Referral: General surgery — urgent elective or emergency.

Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV (intravenous) TDS (three times daily) — Strangulated hernia with bowel compromise

Femoral hernias have the highest strangulation risk of any hernia — urgent elective repair.
Arise below and lateral to the pubic tubercle (distinguish from inguinal — above and medial).
McEvedy or Lockwood approach for elective; low threshold for bowel resection if strangulated.
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Look for sepsis, hypoperfusion or ischaemia (e.g. mesenteric); repeat lactate
• Do not attempt manual reduction when strangulation is suspected (WSES 2017): emergency repair with assessment of bowel viability.
• Emergency Theatre: irreducible / strangulated hernia — bowel resection risk, consent accordingly.
• Consent: hernia repair — recurrence (1–2% TAPP), chronic groin pain (5%), mesh infection (< 1%), testicular ischaemia/vas injury (< 1%), haematoma.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PRE-OPERATIVE:
• Fasting: food up to 6 h and clear fluids up to 2 h before anaesthesia (AAGBI 2010; ESA 2011). Consent signed.
• Antibiotic prophylaxis: single dose at induction per the local antimicrobial policy (emergency repair; possible contamination …(truncated)
• NG tube (16Fr): free drainage + 4-hourly aspiration. Document aspirate volume and character.
• IV Hartmann's 1–2L + IDC — fluid balance, electrolyte replacement (check K⁺ daily).
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast — level (SBO/LBO), transition point, closed loop, ischaemia (pneumatosis).

BOWEL OBSTRUCTION — OPERATIVE PLAN (if conservative fails or signs of ischaemia)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
INDICATIONS FOR SURGERY:
• Signs of bowel ischaemia (peritonism, lactate rising, pneumatosis on CT)
• Closed-loop obstruction on CT
• Complete SBO failing conservative management > 48h
• Strangulating hernia as cause

• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
No routine coagulation test with standard DOAC interruption (PAUSE; ACCP 2022)

• apixaban: high-bleeding-risk procedure — omit for the interval set by drug and creatinine clearance (PAUSE; BSG/ESGE 2021). Low-risk endoscopy — omit the morning dose only. No LMWH bridging for a DOAC.

• No routine LMWH bridging for atrial fibrillation (BRIDGE trial; ACCP 2022); bridging only for high thrombotic risk (e.g. mechanical mitral valve, VTE in the last 3 months), decided with haematology.
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.

management.text: Elective Hernia Repair
Pre-operative assessment and consent. Day-case laparoscopic repair preferred. Antibiotic prophylaxis at induction (cefazolin 1–2 g IV).

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)
[surgical] Emergency repair if strangulation is suspected: resuscitate, IV antibiotics, emergency surgery; assess bowel viability and resect non-viable bowel (WSES 2017).
[surgical] Elective: Lichtenstein mesh herniorrhaphy (local or GA) or laparoscopic TEP/TAPP.
[followup] Review wound at 2 weeks; counsel on recurrence risk and mesh awareness.

management.text: EMERGENCY — Strangulated Hernia
Emergency laparoscopic/open hernia repair. Assess bowel viability — resect if necrotic (primary anastomosis vs stoma based on contamination).
Do NOT delay for imaging if clinical peritonism is present.
- β-HCG: result required before surgery, ionising imaging or a drug that is unsafe in pregnancy — do not record it as negative without a result.

- Known or suspected obstructive sleep apnoea (STOP-Bang ≥ 5): anaesthetic review before listing; bring CPAP; opioid-sparing analgesia; continuous pulse oximetry after surgery; consider a sleep study (SAMBA 2012; ASA 2014).

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)

- Emergency laparotomy / high-risk surgery: document the predicted mortality risk pre-operatively (NELA risk calculator or P-POSSUM); if ≥ 5%, consultant surgeon and anaesthetist present and planned post-operative critical care (NELA; RCS 2018 The Higher Risk General Surgical Patient). Age ≥ 65 or frail: elderly-medicine (geriatric) review.
- Sulfonylurea (gliclazide): omit on the day of the procedure; capillary glucose monitoring, target 6–12 mmol/L (CPOC 2021).
- Metformin: continue if only one meal is missed; omit if more than one meal will be missed, eGFR < 60 mL/min or IV contrast is planned (CPOC 2021).
[surgical] Elective open: Mayo repair or mesh repair (sublay / onlay) depending on defect size.
[surgical] Laparoscopic IPOM (intra-peritoneal on-lay mesh) for large defects.
[surgical] Emergency repair if strangulation is suspected (tender, irreducible, skin change, raised lactate) — WSES 2017.

EMERGENCY VENTRAL (UMBILICAL / PARAUMBILICAL / INCISIONAL) HERNIA REPAIR — OPERATIVE PLAN
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PRE-OPERATIVE:
• Fasting: food up to 6 h and clear fluids up to 2 h before anaesthesia (AAGBI 2010; ESA 2011).
• Antibiotic prophylaxis: single dose at induction per the local antimicrobial policy (emergency repair; possible contamina …(truncated)
• Obstructive sleep apnoea (STOP-Bang): anaesthetic pre-assessment; bring CPAP; opioid-sparing analgesia and post-operative monitoring plan.
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• VTE risk assessment on admission (NICE NG89).
• Mechanical prophylaxis: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression unless contraindicated (NICE NG89).
• Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH unless bleeding risk outweighs it (dose adjusted for renal function); extended to 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery (NICE NG89).
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine albumin:creatinine ratio — diabetic nephropathy screening.
Result action — Lactate 2.9 mmol/L: Lactate 2-4 mmol/L — Raised lactate: repeat within 2-4 h and look for sepsis, bleeding or ischaemia (SSC 2021).
Score action — NEWS2 1: Low — NEWS2 1-4: minimum 4-6-hourly observations; registered nurse assessment and decision on escalation (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 0: Below 2 — qSOFA < 2 does not exclude sepsis: continue NEWS2 monitoring and reassess if infection is suspected (Sepsis-3; SSC 2021 advises against qSOFA alone as a screening tool).

management.text: [immediate] Severe symptoms (seizure, reduced consciousness): Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.

[immediate] Severe symptoms: 150 mL 3% hypertonic saline IV over 20 minutes; recheck serum sodium at 20 minutes; repeat up to twice until sodium has risen by 5 mmol/L; HDU/ICU (European guideline 2014).
[immediate] Stop hypotonic IV fluids (5% glucose / dextrose 5%, 0.18% saline) — especially after surgery (NICE CG174).
[immediate] Stop thiazide diuretics (bendroflumethiazide, indapamide) and other causative drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine) where possible.
[conservative] Hypovolaemic (e.g. high-output ileostomy, vomiting): restore volume with IV 0.9% saline or balanced crystalloid 0.5–1 mL/kg/h — do not fluid-restrict.

• Assess volume status first: hypovolaemic → isotonic saline; euvolaemic (SIADH) → fluid restriction; stop thiazides and other causative drugs
• Stop hypotonic IV fluids (e.g. 5% glucose, 0.18% saline) — NICE CG174 / NPSA
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• 12-lead ECG (cardiac cause of transient loss of consciousness — NICE CG109 / NG217)
• Urgent referral to a first-seizure clinic / neurologist, seen within 2 weeks (NICE NG217)
• Driving safety advice: stop driving and inform the licensing authority; avoid unsupervised swimming and working at heights until reviewed

• Assess with the 4AT; look for and treat the cause: sepsis / anastomotic leak, hypoxia, pain, urinary retention, constipation, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics), electrolytes, alcohol withdrawal (NICE CG103)
• If urine β-HCG positive: serum quantitative β-HCG + urgent TVS — exclude ectopic.
• If ectopic suspected: emergency gynaecology referral — surgical or medical management.
• Urine Na (> 20: SIADH/renal loss; < 20: hypovolaemic/oedematous states), urine osmolality, serum osmolality.
• Review medications for SIADH causes: diuretics, SSRIs, carbamazepine.
• Exclude secondary SIADH causes: CXR (lung malignancy), CT head (CNS lesion/meningitis).

• Assess volume status first (European guideline 2014): hypovolaemic (e.g. high stoma output, vomiting) → IV 0.9% sodium chloride, not fluid restriction; euvolaemic SIADH → restrict fluids; limit the rise to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h.
• Severe symptoms only: 150 mL 3% hypertonic saline IV over 20 minutes, recheck Na⁺, repeat up to twice aiming for a 5 mmol/L rise (European guideline 2014) — HDU / endocrinology.
• Stop thiazide / thiazide-like diuretics and review SSRIs, carbamazepine and other causative drugs.
• Elective surgery deferred — sodium < 130 mmol/L anaesthetic risk; target ≥ 130 pre-op.
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Low potassium or sodium, dehydration or chronic constipation — ask about detox teas and cleanses: asked.
• Document date and result of last cervical screening test.
• Cervical screening: primary HPV test every 5 years (USPSTF 2018 / WHO 2021); cytology every 3 years if HPV testing unavailable.

Left-sided obstruction: resection (Hartmann's procedure, or primary anastomosis ± defunctioning stoma), SEMS as a bridge to elective resection where expertise exists (not if perforation, ischaemia or peritonitis), or a defunctioning colostomy; palliative SEMS for incurable disease.

management.text: Large Bowel Obstruction — Malignant
CT staging. Colorectal/Oncology MDT referral.
Stent (SEMS) contraindicated with perforation, peritonitis or impending caecal perforation (tender, dilated caecum — ischaemia): emergency resection instead (WSES 2018; ESGE 2020).
Right-sided / transverse obstruction: right (or extended right) hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis when physiology allows.

Left-sided obstruction: resection (Hartmann's procedure, or primary anastomosis ± defunctioning stoma), SEMS as a bridge to elective resection where expertise exists (not if perforation, ischaemia or peritonitis), or a defunctioning colostomy; palliative SEMS for incurable disease.
Decision based on: perforation risk, patient fitness, tumour stage, institutional expertise.

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)

- Emergency laparotomy / high-risk surgery: document the predicted mortality risk pre-operatively (NELA risk calculator or P-POSSUM); if ≥ 5%, consultant surgeon and anaesthetist present and planned post-operative critical care (NELA; RCS 2018 The Higher Risk General Surgical Patient). Age ≥ 65 or frail: elderly-medicine (geriatric) review.
- Metformin: continue if only one meal is missed; omit if more than one meal will be missed, eGFR < 60 mL/min or IV contrast is planned (CPOC 2021).

[surgical] Colon cancer: laparoscopic or open resection by tumour site with D3 lymphadenectomy — right (or extended right) hemicolectomy for right-sided tumours; left hemicolectomy or sigmoid colectomy if left-sided.
[surgical] Obstructing right-sided or transverse cancer: right (or extended right) hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis in most patients (WSES 2018).

[surgical] Obstructing left-sided cancer: resection with anastomosis ± defunctioning stoma, Hartmann's procedure, or a colonic stent (SEMS) as a bridge — stenting is contraindicated with perforation, impending caecal perforation (tender caecum, ischaemia) or peritonitis (WSES 2018; ESGE 2020).
[surgical] Rectal cancer: anterior resection (or APR for low tumours); TEMS / TEM for T1 disease.
[followup] Surveillance colonoscopy at 1 year, then 3-yearly; CEA + CT at 6-monthly intervals × 3 years.

Pyogenic (E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococcus) commonest in Caribbean; amoebic (E. histolytica) in travellers.
Single right lobe abscess is typical; CT liver with contrast is the diagnostic standard.
USS-guided percutaneous aspiration / drainage is the primary intervention.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Act on the critical result now: senior review, repeat and identify the cause
• Defer elective surgery — coronary stent / ACS 5 months ago is inside the 6-month dual antiplatelet window (ESC/ESAIC 2022). Do not stop antiplatelets without cardiology.
• Cardiology liaison: timing of surgery and antiplatelet management.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Meropenem 1g TDS + Vancomycin 25mg/kg (septic shock — broad cover).
• IV fluid resuscitation: 30ml/kg Hartmann's bolus — reassess lactate and BP at 30 min.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Vasopressors: Noradrenaline 0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min if MAP < 65 after 30ml/kg fluid.
• HDU/ICU admission — continuous BP monitoring, lactate trend.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• USS abdomen — biliary tree, gallstones, hepatic parenchyma.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• MRCP — CBD diameter, stone burden, biliary stricture characterisation.
• ERCP only if MRCP / EUS confirms an obstructing stone or stricture — therapeutic stone extraction or stenting.
• HPB surgical review if a mass or stricture is found.
• Supplemental O₂: titrate to SpO₂ 94–98% (BTS 2017); reassess.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• Urine protein:creatinine ratio — nephrotic syndrome (PCR > 300mg/mmol).
• Dietitian referral — pre-operative nutritional support. Delay elective surgery ≥ 4 weeks if possible.
• Prescribe ONS (Ensure/Fortisip) ×2 — pre-op nutritional optimisation (ERAS).
• If albumin < 25 g/L and surgery urgent: parenteral nutrition pre-operatively with nutrition team support.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ACR — hypertensive nephropathy screen.
• Document bilateral BP — coarctation exclusion if > 20mmHg differential.
• Fever or skin / line-site infection — ask about IV drips: asked.

If suspected infection, sepsis bundle now: blood cultures and IV antibiotics within 1 h (SSC 2021).

Score action — NEWS2 15: High — NEWS2 >= 7: continuous monitoring and an emergency response by a team with critical-care skills; consider HDU/ICU. In the clinic, call 911 for transfer to the nearest emergency department (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 3: 2 or more — qSOFA >= 2: high risk of a poor outcome. If suspected infection, treat as sepsis: lactate, blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 h, fluid resuscitation guided by perfusion and senior review (SSC 2021); otherwise look for another cause of organ dysfunction.
