[immediate] Ruptured AAA: two large-bore IV cannulae, cross-match 6 units RBC, permissive hypotension (systolic 70–90 mmHg while conscious) — avoid large fluid boluses; blood products rather than crystalloid (ESVS 2024).
[surgical] Ruptured or symptomatic AAA: immediate vascular surgery — emergency EVAR where anatomy allows, otherwise open repair (ESVS 2024).
[surgical] Elective repair for AAA ≥5.5 cm (men) / ≥5.0 cm (women), or symptomatic/rapidly expanding: EVAR preferred where anatomy permits.
[surgical] Open surgical repair (midline laparotomy, aortic graft) for anatomy unsuitable for EVAR or EVAR failure.
[conservative] Small AAA (3.0–5.4 cm): surveillance ultrasound 3-yearly (3–4.4 cm) or annually (4.5–5.4 cm).
[conservative] Cardiovascular risk reduction: statin, antiplatelet, smoking cessation, blood pressure control.
[followup] Post-EVAR: CT at 1 month, 12 months, then annually for endoleak surveillance.

management.text: - VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)

[immediate] Suspected ectopic pregnancy seen in clinic (pain, bleeding or collapse with a positive pregnancy test): Outpatient clinic: obstetric emergency — call 911 or arrange immediate transfer to a hospital with an obstetric unit (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); inform the on-call obstetric team before arrival.
[immediate] Resuscitation: two large-bore IV cannulae; IV fluids; O2; crossmatch; urgent gynaecology review.
[surgical] Ruptured/haemodynamically unstable: emergency surgery — laparoscopy (salpingectomy), laparotomy if unstable; methotrexate and expectant management are contraindicated (NICE NG126).
[surgical] Unruptured ectopic with haemodynamic stability: laparoscopic salpingectomy (preferred) or salpingostomy (if contralateral tube damaged).

[conservative] Medical management with methotrexate (50 mg/m² IM, single dose) only for selected unruptured ectopics: haemodynamically stable, no significant pain, adnexal mass < 35 mm with no visible heartbeat, serum hCG < 1500 IU/L (may be offered up to 5000 IU/L), able to attend follow-up (NICE NG126).
[conservative] Expectant management only for clinically stable, pain-free women with a tubal ectopic < 35 mm, no visible heartbeat and serum hCG ≤ 1000 IU/L, with close follow-up (NICE NG126).

[followup] Serial β-hCG until negative when an unruptured ectopic was managed medically or expectantly (urine pregnancy test at 3 weeks after salpingectomy); anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU for rhesus-negative women having surgery for an ectopic pregnancy (NICE NG126).

Classic triad: amenorrhoea, lower abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding — but only 50% present classically.
Positive β-hCG with empty uterus on transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) = ectopic until proven otherwise.
Ruptured ectopic is a life-threatening emergency: shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation, haemodynamic collapse.
Ruptured or haemodynamically unstable ectopic: methotrexate and expectant management are contraindicated — emergency surgery (NICE NG126).
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Immediate gynaecology referral; haemodynamically unstable → emergency surgery (NICE NG126)
• If urine β-HCG positive: serum quantitative β-HCG + urgent TVS — exclude ectopic.
• If ectopic suspected: emergency gynaecology referral — surgical or medical management.
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• IV fluid challenge 500ml if hypovolaemia likely — reassess HR at 30 min.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements

Score action — NEWS2 3: Low — NEWS2 1-4: minimum 4-6-hourly observations; registered nurse assessment and decision on escalation (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 0: Below 2 — qSOFA < 2 does not exclude sepsis: continue NEWS2 monitoring and reassess if infection is suspected (Sepsis-3; SSC 2021 advises against qSOFA alone as a screening tool).

Atypical presentations are common in women, older people and people with diabetes: epigastric pain, breathlessness, nausea or "indigestion" — record a 12-lead ECG in every adult with unexplained upper abdominal or chest pain.
Inferior STEMI often presents as epigastric pain with vomiting and is mislabelled biliary colic or gastritis.
In pregnancy, spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a leading cause of ACS.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).

• Oxygen only if SpO₂ < 90% (ESC 2023); IV access; continuous ECG monitoring during transfer
• Act on the critical result now: senior review, repeat and identify the cause

• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• Hold beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin — pending cardiology review.

[immediate] Suspected ruptured or symptomatic AAA: Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.

[immediate] Ruptured AAA: two large-bore IV cannulae, cross-match 6 units RBC, permissive hypotension (systolic 70–90 mmHg while conscious) — avoid large fluid boluses; blood products rather than crystalloid (ESVS 2024).
[surgical] Ruptured or symptomatic AAA: immediate vascular surgery — emergency EVAR where anatomy allows, otherwise open repair (ESVS 2024).
[surgical] Elective repair for AAA ≥5.5 cm (men) / ≥5.0 cm (women), or symptomatic/rapidly expanding: EVAR preferred where anatomy permits.
[surgical] Open surgical repair (midline laparotomy, aortic graft) for anatomy unsuitable for EVAR or EVAR failure.
[conservative] Small AAA (3.0–5.4 cm): surveillance ultrasound 3-yearly (3–4.4 cm) or annually (4.5–5.4 cm).

Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)
- Sulfonylurea (gliclazide): omit on the day of the procedure; capillary glucose monitoring, target 6–12 mmol/L (CPOC 2021).
- Metformin: continue if only one meal is missed; omit if more than one meal will be missed, eGFR < 60 mL/min or IV contrast is planned (CPOC 2021).
[immediate] Emergency resuscitation: IV fluids, oxygen; activate major trauma pathway if haemodynamically unstable.
[immediate] Empirical IV antibiotics: meropenem + clindamycin + vancomycin — broad-spectrum pending cultures.

[conservative] Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) as adjunct if available — reduces mortality in some centres.
[followup] HDU / ICU admission; plastic surgery for reconstruction; prolonged antibiotics per cultures.

Life-threatening surgical emergency — mortality 25–35%; every hour's delay worsens outcome.
Type I (polymicrobial — Meleney's, Fournier's) and Type II (Group A Streptococcus) are the two main types.
LRINEC score >6 raises suspicion; do NOT wait for CT or laboratory confirmation if the diagnosis is clinically likely.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Heparin and immediate vascular / general surgical referral for revascularisation (ESVS 2017)
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Emergency surgical exploration and debridement; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; a low LRINEC score does not exclude NSTI (WSES 2018)
• Look for sepsis, hypoperfusion or ischaemia (e.g. mesenteric); repeat lactate
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS — empirical sepsis cover.
• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• Ketones urgently — blood ketones > 3 mmol/L = DKA; urine ketones > 2+ = DKA screen positive.

• If DKA (ketones ≥ 3 mmol/L + pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 15): fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h with potassium replacement (JBDS 2023). If HHS (osmolality ≥ 320, ketones < 3): IV 0.9% sodium chloride first; fixed-rate insulin 0.05 units/kg/h only once glucose stops falling with fluids (JBDS 2022). Monitor K⁺ hourly.
• Defer elective surgery — target glucose 6–10 mmol/L, ketones < 0.5 mmol/L pre-operatively.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ketones — exclude diabetic ketoacidosis.
• Variable-rate insulin infusion (VRIII) if inpatient glucose consistently > 11 mmol/L.
• Diabetology review — adjust long-term insulin/OHG regimen.
• Urine albumin:creatinine ratio — diabetic nephropathy screening.
• Low potassium or sodium, dehydration or chronic constipation — ask about detox teas and cleanses: asked.
• Fever or skin / line-site infection — ask about IV drips: asked.
Result action — Lactate 3.6 mmol/L: Lactate 2-4 mmol/L — Raised lactate: repeat within 2-4 h and look for sepsis, bleeding or ischaemia (SSC 2021).

Score action — NEWS2 8: High — NEWS2 >= 7: continuous monitoring and an emergency response by a team with critical-care skills; consider HDU/ICU. In the clinic, call 911 for transfer to the nearest emergency department (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 2: 2 or more — qSOFA >= 2: high risk of a poor outcome. If suspected infection, treat as sepsis: lactate, blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 h, fluid resuscitation guided by perfusion and senior review (SSC 2021); otherwise look for another cause of organ dysfunction.

Life-threatening surgical emergency — mortality 25–35%; every hour's delay worsens outcome.
Type I (polymicrobial — Meleney's, Fournier's) and Type II (Group A Streptococcus) are the two main types.
LRINEC score >6 raises suspicion; do NOT wait for CT or laboratory confirmation if the diagnosis is clinically likely.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Act on the critical result now: senior review, repeat and identify the cause
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Emergency surgical exploration and debridement; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; a low LRINEC score does not exclude NSTI (WSES 2018)
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).

• No routine LMWH bridging for atrial fibrillation (BRIDGE trial; ACCP 2022); bridging only for high thrombotic risk (e.g. mechanical mitral valve, VTE in the last 3 months), decided with haematology.
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.

• ⚠ PENICILLIN ALLERGY recorded — the penicillin-class antibiotic proposed here is withheld: use a non-penicillin alternative per the local antimicrobial guideline (after anaphylaxis, avoid cephalosporins and carbapenems too unless allergy advice says otherwise).
• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• VTE risk assessment on admission (NICE NG89).
• Mechanical prophylaxis: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression unless contraindicated (NICE NG89).
• Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH unless bleeding risk outweighs it (dose adjusted for renal function); extended to 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery (NICE NG89).
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ACR — hypertensive nephropathy screen.
• Document bilateral BP — coarctation exclusion if > 20mmHg differential.
• Low potassium or sodium, dehydration or chronic constipation — ask about detox teas and cleanses: asked.
• Fever or skin / line-site infection — ask about IV drips: asked.
• Colorectal cancer screening offered (USPSTF 2021, age 45–75): FIT every year or colonoscopy every 10 years — choice documented.
• Document date of last screening mammogram.
• Screening mammogram every 2 years (biennial, USPSTF 2024, age 40–74).
• Diabetes screening (ADA 2024): HbA1c or fasting glucose; repeat every 3 years if normal, yearly if prediabetes.
• Calculate 10-year cardiovascular (ASCVD) risk — statin discussion if ≥ 10% with a risk factor (USPSTF 2022).
• DXA bone density scan — osteoporosis screening (USPSTF 2018, women ≥ 65).
• Estimate 10-year fracture risk (FRAX).

If suspected infection, sepsis bundle now: blood cultures and IV antibiotics within 1 h (SSC 2021).

Score action — NEWS2 10: High — NEWS2 >= 7: continuous monitoring and an emergency response by a team with critical-care skills; consider HDU/ICU. In the clinic, call 911 for transfer to the nearest emergency department (RCP NEWS2 2017).

management.text: [immediate] Outpatient clinic: obstetric emergency — call 911 or arrange immediate transfer to a hospital with an obstetric unit (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); inform the on-call obstetric team before arrival.
[immediate] Treat severe hypertension: labetalol (oral or IV) first line; nifedipine or IV hydralazine as alternatives — target BP ≤ 135/85 mmHg (NICE NG133).

[immediate] Eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia: magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 5–15 minutes, then 1 g/h for 24 h; further 2–4 g over 5–15 minutes for a recurrent seizure (Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen, NICE NG133). Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output.
[immediate] Eclamptic seizure: airway, left lateral position, oxygen; magnesium sulfate (not diazepam) first line.
[conservative] Severe pre-eclampsia: limit maintenance fluids to 80 mL/h unless there are ongoing losses (NICE NG133).
[surgical] Timing and mode of delivery by the obstetric team once the mother is stabilised (delivery is the definitive treatment).
[followup] Postpartum: continue antihypertensive treatment — choice with the obstetric team, compatible with breastfeeding (NICE NG133); pre-eclampsia can present up to 6 weeks after birth.

[immediate] Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.

[immediate] Adults: IV 0.9% sodium chloride — [fluids by weight — calculate per APLS/BNFc (mL/kg)] over the first hour ([fluids by weight — calculate per APLS/BNFc (mL/kg)] over 10–15 min if SBP < 90 mmHg), then per the JBDS fluid schedule, adjusted for age, heart failure and renal failure.
[immediate] Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (FRIII) 0.1 units/kg/h (JBDS 2023).
[immediate] Continue long-acting (basal) insulin at the usual dose throughout (JBDS 2023).
[immediate] Potassium replacement in each litre of fluid by serum K⁺: > 5.5 mmol/L none; 3.5–5.5 mmol/L potassium chloride 40 mmol/L; < 3.5 mmol/L senior review for additional potassium (JBDS 2023).
[immediate] Add 10% glucose at [fluids by weight — calculate per APLS/BNFc (mL/kg)] alongside the saline when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L — from the start in euglycaemic DKA (JBDS 2023).
[immediate] Stop any SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin); do not restart without specialist review (MHRA).
[immediate] Children and young people: follow the BSPED 2021 DKA protocol (different fluid volumes and insulin timing); hourly neurological observations for cerebral oedema; paediatric team.

management.text: Mild Acute Pancreatitis — Supportive Management
Moderate, goal-directed IV fluids (lactated Ringer's / Hartmann's) — avoid aggressive fluids (WATERFALL 2022; ACG 2024). Pain control. Early oral feeding as tolerated. No prophylactic antibiotics.
Address aetiology: USS (gallstones → laparoscopic cholecystectomy same admission if mild pancreatitis).

[immediate] Moderate goal-directed IV fluids with lactated Ringer's / Hartmann's: 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h, reassessed at 12, 24 and 48 h — avoid aggressive fluids (WATERFALL 2022; ACG 2024); reduce with heart failure or CKD.
[immediate] Analgesia: IV opioid (morphine) with antiemetic; paracetamol.
[immediate] Early oral feeding within 24 h as tolerated (low-fat solid diet); enteral (NG/NJ) feeding if oral intake is not tolerated — not parenteral (ACG 2024).
[immediate] No prophylactic antibiotics; antibiotics only for documented or strongly suspected infection (infected necrosis, cholangitis, pneumonia, UTI) — ACG 2024.
[conservative] Biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis: ERCP within 24 h (ACG 2024; TG18); ERCP is not routine without cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction.

[conservative] Mild biliary pancreatitis: laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones during the same admission (ACG 2024); with peripancreatic collections or necrosis, defer cholecystectomy until collections resolve or beyond 6 weeks (IAP/APA 2013).
[conservative] Alcohol-related: thiamine (IV Pabrinex or oral) and alcohol-withdrawal assessment and treatment per local protocol (e.g. CIWA-Ar-guided chlordiazepoxide); alcohol cessation support.
[conservative] Drug-induced (e.g. azathioprine): stop the causative drug and record it as an adverse reaction; do not rechallenge.

[conservative] Hypertriglyceridaemia (> 11.3 mmol/L): specialist management (insulin–glucose infusion; plasmapheresis in selected cases), then triglyceride-lowering therapy; no cholecystectomy unless gallstones are present.
[conservative] Severe disease: HDU/ICU; monitor intra-abdominal (bladder) pressure for abdominal compartment syndrome.
[followup] Interval cholecystectomy for gallstone aetiology if not done in-patient (after collections resolve).
[followup] Pancreatic function testing (exocrine / endocrine) after severe episode.

management.text: Mild Acute Pancreatitis — Supportive Management
Moderate, goal-directed IV fluids (lactated Ringer's / Hartmann's) — avoid aggressive fluids (WATERFALL 2022; ACG 2024). Pain control. Early oral feeding as tolerated. No prophylactic antibiotics.
Address aetiology: USS (gallstones → laparoscopic cholecystectomy same admission if mild pancreatitis).
- β-HCG: result required before surgery, ionising imaging or a drug that is unsafe in pregnancy — do not record it as negative without a result.

- Long-term glucocorticoid (prednisolone): do not stop it. If ≥ 5 mg prednisolone (or equivalent) for > 4 weeks, give steroid cover — hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction or at the start of the acute illness, then 200 mg/24 h (infusion, or 50 mg IV/IM 6-hourly) while unwell or nil by mouth, then double the usual oral dose for 48 h (AAGBI/Society for Endocrinology 2020).
- Immunosuppressed (azathioprine, prednisolone): fever, peritonism and a raised white cell count may be blunted — lower threshold for imaging, senior review and escalation.

[immediate] Moderate goal-directed IV fluids with lactated Ringer's / Hartmann's: 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h, reassessed at 12, 24 and 48 h — avoid aggressive fluids (WATERFALL 2022; ACG 2024); reduce with heart failure or CKD.
[immediate] Analgesia: IV opioid (morphine) with antiemetic; paracetamol.
[immediate] Early oral feeding within 24 h as tolerated (low-fat solid diet); enteral (NG/NJ) feeding if oral intake is not tolerated — not parenteral (ACG 2024).
[immediate] No prophylactic antibiotics; antibiotics only for documented or strongly suspected infection (infected necrosis, cholangitis, pneumonia, UTI) — ACG 2024.
[conservative] Biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis: ERCP within 24 h (ACG 2024; TG18); ERCP is not routine without cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction.

[conservative] Mild biliary pancreatitis: laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones during the same admission (ACG 2024); with peripancreatic collections or necrosis, defer cholecystectomy until collections resolve or beyond 6 weeks (IAP/APA 2013).
[conservative] Alcohol-related: thiamine (IV Pabrinex or oral) and alcohol-withdrawal assessment and treatment per local protocol (e.g. CIWA-Ar-guided chlordiazepoxide); alcohol cessation support.
[conservative] Drug-induced (e.g. azathioprine): stop the causative drug and record it as an adverse reaction; do not rechallenge.

[conservative] Hypertriglyceridaemia (> 11.3 mmol/L): specialist management (insulin–glucose infusion; plasmapheresis in selected cases), then triglyceride-lowering therapy; no cholecystectomy unless gallstones are present.
[conservative] Severe disease: HDU/ICU; monitor intra-abdominal (bladder) pressure for abdominal compartment syndrome.
[followup] Interval cholecystectomy for gallstone aetiology if not done in-patient (after collections resolve).
[followup] Pancreatic function testing (exocrine / endocrine) after severe episode.

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. On therapeutic anticoagulation: see the anticoagulation plan; while it is interrupted after surgery use mechanical prophylaxis and prophylactic-dose LMWH when bleeding risk allows.
- Beta-blocker (bisoprolol): tachycardia may be blunted — heart rate can under-read shock or sepsis (ATLS 10).

[immediate] Moderate goal-directed IV fluids with lactated Ringer's / Hartmann's: 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h, reassessed at 12, 24 and 48 h — avoid aggressive fluids (WATERFALL 2022; ACG 2024); reduce with heart failure or CKD.
[immediate] Analgesia: IV opioid (morphine) with antiemetic; paracetamol.
[immediate] Early oral feeding within 24 h as tolerated (low-fat solid diet); enteral (NG/NJ) feeding if oral intake is not tolerated — not parenteral (ACG 2024).
[immediate] No prophylactic antibiotics; antibiotics only for documented or strongly suspected infection (infected necrosis, cholangitis, pneumonia, UTI) — ACG 2024.
[conservative] Biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis: ERCP within 24 h (ACG 2024; TG18); ERCP is not routine without cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction.

[conservative] Mild biliary pancreatitis: laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones during the same admission (ACG 2024); with peripancreatic collections or necrosis, defer cholecystectomy until collections resolve or beyond 6 weeks (IAP/APA 2013).
[conservative] Alcohol-related: thiamine (IV Pabrinex or oral) and alcohol-withdrawal assessment and treatment per local protocol (e.g. CIWA-Ar-guided chlordiazepoxide); alcohol cessation support.
[conservative] Drug-induced (e.g. azathioprine): stop the causative drug and record it as an adverse reaction; do not rechallenge.

[conservative] Hypertriglyceridaemia (> 11.3 mmol/L): specialist management (insulin–glucose infusion; plasmapheresis in selected cases), then triglyceride-lowering therapy; no cholecystectomy unless gallstones are present.
[conservative] Severe disease: HDU/ICU; monitor intra-abdominal (bladder) pressure for abdominal compartment syndrome.
[surgical] Infected necrosis (CECT gas or FNA confirmed): step-up approach — percutaneous or endoscopic drainage → minimally invasive necrosectomy, delayed ≥ 4 weeks until walled off.
[followup] Interval cholecystectomy for gallstone aetiology if not done in-patient (after collections resolve).
[followup] Pancreatic function testing (exocrine / endocrine) after severe episode.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA): defined as aortic diameter >3 cm; risk of rupture rises sharply above 5.5 cm (men) and 5.0 cm (women).
Rupture presents as triad of hypotension, back/abdominal pain, and pulsatile abdominal mass — mortality without surgery >90%.
Symptomatic or rapidly expanding AAA (>1 cm/year or >0.5 cm/6 months) warrants urgent repair regardless of size.
A first episode of "renal colic" over 60 without a stone history is a leaking AAA until the aorta has been imaged (bedside ultrasound / CT angiography).

management.text: Severe Acute Pancreatitis — ICU Level Care
ICU admission. Goal-directed resuscitation with moderate fluids — avoid aggressive fluids (WATERFALL 2022; ACG 2024). Enteral feeding via NGT/NJT within 24–48 h (superior to TPN).
Carbapenem antibiotics (meropenem) ONLY if infected necrosis suspected (fever + gas in necrotic area on CT).
Necrosectomy: step-up approach (endoscopic > percutaneous > surgical) — delayed ≥4 weeks until walled-off.

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)

[immediate] Analgesia: IV opioid (morphine) with antiemetic; paracetamol.
[immediate] Early oral feeding within 24 h as tolerated (low-fat solid diet); enteral (NG/NJ) feeding if oral intake is not tolerated — not parenteral (ACG 2024).

[followup] Interval cholecystectomy for gallstone aetiology if not done in-patient (after collections resolve).
[followup] Pancreatic function testing (exocrine / endocrine) after severe episode.

expectations.note: WATERFALL (NEJM 2022) was stopped for harm: aggressive resuscitation (20 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg/h) caused more fluid overload (20.5% vs 6.3%) without benefit. ACG 2024 recommends moderate, goal-directed fluids. A plan that says "aggressive" or 250–500 mL/h is a fluid-overload hazard. In established organ failure with respiratory failure and pleural effusions, fluid overload worsens outcome.

Most commonly caused by single parathyroid adenoma (~85%); presents with hypercalcaemia, often incidentally discovered.
Classic mnemonic "bones, stones, groans, psychic moans": osteoporosis, renal stones, constipation, depression/fatigue.
Surgical cure rate >95% with minimally invasive parathyroidectomy guided by pre-operative localisation.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV 0.9% sodium chloride rehydration (Society for Endocrinology 2016)
• IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid or pamidronate) after rehydration, adjusted for renal function (Society for Endocrinology 2016)
• Stop thiazides, calcium and vitamin D supplements
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ACR — hypertensive nephropathy screen.
• Document bilateral BP — coarctation exclusion if > 20mmHg differential.
• Low potassium or sodium, dehydration or chronic constipation — ask about detox teas and cleanses: asked.

• Consent: laparoscopic cholecystectomy — bile duct injury (0.3%), haemorrhage, conversion to open, bile leak, retained stone, wound infection.

LAPAROSCOPIC CHOLECYSTECTOMY — OPERATIVE PLAN
─────────────────────────────────────────────
PRE-OPERATIVE:
• Fasting: food up to 6 h and clear fluids up to 2 h before anaesthesia (AAGBI 2010; ESA 2011).
• Antibiotic prophylaxis not indicated for low-risk elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy (SIGN 104); a single dose if the operation becomes high-risk (conversion, bile spillage, chol …(truncated)
• VTE risk assessment on admission (NICE NG89).
• Mechanical prophylaxis: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression unless contraindicated (NICE NG89).
• Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH unless bleeding risk outweighs it (dose adjusted for renal function); extended to 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery (NICE NG89).
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ACR — hypertensive nephropathy screen.
• Document bilateral BP — coarctation exclusion if > 20mmHg differential.
• Colorectal cancer screening offered (USPSTF 2021, age 45–75): FIT every year or colonoscopy every 10 years — choice documented.
• Document date of last screening mammogram.
• Screening mammogram every 2 years (biennial, USPSTF 2024, age 40–74).
• Diabetes screening (ADA 2024): HbA1c or fasting glucose; repeat every 3 years if normal, yearly if prediabetes.
• Calculate 10-year cardiovascular (ASCVD) risk — statin discussion if ≥ 10% with a risk factor (USPSTF 2022).
• DXA bone density scan — osteoporosis screening (USPSTF 2018, women ≥ 65).
• Estimate 10-year fracture risk (FRAX).

[immediate] Add 10% glucose at 125 mL/h alongside the saline when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L — from the start in euglycaemic DKA (JBDS 2023).

- SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin): withhold the day before and the day of the procedure (CPOC 2021; FDA labelling advises 3 days, 4 for ertugliflozin — surgeon to choose); check blood ketones before and after, even if glucose is normal; restart when eating and drinking normally.

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)
- Sulfonylurea (gliclazide): omit on the day of the procedure; capillary glucose monitoring, target 6–12 mmol/L (CPOC 2021).
- Metformin: continue if only one meal is missed; omit if more than one meal will be missed, eGFR < 60 mL/min or IV contrast is planned (CPOC 2021).
[immediate] Irreducible, tender hernia: nil by mouth, IV fluids and analgesia; assess for strangulation (skin changes, peritonism, systemic toxicity, raised lactate) — WSES 2017.

[conservative] Incarcerated without any sign of strangulation: a single gentle reduction by an experienced surgeon with analgesia may be considered; do not attempt reduction if strangulation is suspected (WSES 2017). If reduced, admit and repair on the same admission.

[conservative] Minimally symptomatic, reducible inguinal hernia in men who decline or are unfit for repair: watchful waiting after discussion — not for women (femoral hernia risk) or an irreducible hernia; most eventually choose repair (HerniaSurge 2018).
[surgical] Emergency repair if strangulation is suspected: resuscitate, IV antibiotics, emergency surgery; assess bowel viability and resect non-viable bowel (WSES 2017).
[surgical] Elective: Lichtenstein mesh herniorrhaphy (local or GA) or laparoscopic TEP/TAPP.
[followup] Review wound at 2 weeks; counsel on recurrence risk and mesh awareness.

• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Look for sepsis, hypoperfusion or ischaemia (e.g. mesenteric); repeat lactate
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).

• No routine LMWH bridging for atrial fibrillation (BRIDGE trial; ACCP 2022); bridging only for high thrombotic risk (e.g. mechanical mitral valve, VTE in the last 3 months), decided with haematology.
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS — empirical sepsis cover.
• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.

Score action — qSOFA 1: Below 2 — qSOFA < 2 does not exclude sepsis: continue NEWS2 monitoring and reassess if infection is suspected (Sepsis-3; SSC 2021 advises against qSOFA alone as a screening tool).

SSI is classified as superficial incisional, deep incisional, or organ/space — organ/space SSI (e.g. anastomotic leak) is most serious.
S. aureus (including MRSA) is the commonest pathogen; bowel surgery adds gram-negatives and anaerobes.
CDC criteria: infection within 30 days (or 90 days if implant) — purulent discharge, culture positive, or clinician diagnosis.
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for high risk when infection is the likely cause (NICE NG51)
• IV fluid resuscitation per NICE NG51 unless heart failure or pulmonary oedema is recorded; senior review
• Look for sepsis, hypoperfusion or ischaemia (e.g. mesenteric); repeat lactate
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).

• No routine LMWH bridging for atrial fibrillation (BRIDGE trial; ACCP 2022); bridging only for high thrombotic risk (e.g. mechanical mitral valve, VTE in the last 3 months), decided with haematology.
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.
• IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS — empirical sepsis cover.
• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.
• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.
• Ketones urgently — blood ketones > 3 mmol/L = DKA; urine ketones > 2+ = DKA screen positive.

• If DKA (ketones ≥ 3 mmol/L + pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 15): fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h with potassium replacement (JBDS 2023). If HHS (osmolality ≥ 320, ketones < 3): IV 0.9% sodium chloride first; fixed-rate insulin 0.05 units/kg/h only once glucose stops falling with fluids (JBDS 2022). Monitor K⁺ hourly.
• Defer elective surgery — target glucose 6–10 mmol/L, ketones < 0.5 mmol/L pre-operatively.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Urine ketones — exclude diabetic ketoacidosis.
• Variable-rate insulin infusion (VRIII) if inpatient glucose consistently > 11 mmol/L.
• Diabetology review — adjust long-term insulin/OHG regimen.
• Urine albumin:creatinine ratio — diabetic nephropathy screening.
• Fever or skin / line-site infection — ask about IV drips: asked.
• PSA screening discussed (USPSTF 2018): benefits and harms explained; patient's informed decision documented.
Order a PSA only if the patient chooses screening after the discussion

management.text: [for this patient] VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. [immediate] Moderate goal-directed IV fluids with lactated Ringer's / Hartmann's: 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h, reassessed at 12, 24 and 48 h — avoid aggressive fluids (WATERFALL 2022; ACG 2024); reduce with heart failure or CKD.
[immediate] Analgesia: IV opioid (morphine) with antiemetic; paracetamol.
[immediate] Early oral feeding within 24 h as tolerated (low-fat solid diet); enteral (NG/NJ) feeding if oral intake is not tolerated — not parenteral (ACG 2024).
[immediate] No prophylactic antibiotics; antibiotics only for documented or strongly suspected infection (infected necrosis, cholangitis, pneumonia, UTI) — ACG 2024.
[conservative] Biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis: ERCP within 24 h (ACG 2024; TG18); ERCP is not routine without cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction.

[conservative] Mild biliary pancreatitis: laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones during the same admission (ACG 2024); with peripancreatic collections or necrosis, defer cholecystectomy until collections resolve or beyond 6 weeks (IAP/APA 2013).
[conservative] Alcohol-related: thiamine (IV Pabrinex or oral) and alcohol-withdrawal assessment and treatment per local protocol (e.g. CIWA-Ar-guided chlordiazepoxide); alcohol cessation support.
[conservative] Drug-induced (e.g. azathioprine): stop the causative drug and record it as an adverse reaction; do not rechallenge.

[conservative] Hypertriglyceridaemia (> 11.3 mmol/L): specialist management (insulin–glucose infusion; plasmapheresis in selected cases), then triglyceride-lowering therapy; no cholecystectomy unless gallstones are present.
[conservative] Severe disease: HDU/ICU; monitor intra-abdominal (bladder) pressure for abdominal compartment syndrome.
[surgical] Infected necrosis (CECT gas or FNA confirmed): step-up approach — percutaneous or endoscopic drainage → minimally invasive necrosectomy, delayed ≥ 4 weeks until walled off.
[followup] Interval cholecystectomy for gallstone aetiology if not done in-patient (after collections resolve).
[followup] Pancreatic function testing (exocrine / endocrine) after severe episode.
Moderate, goal-directed fluids — high-volume fluid resuscitation increases fluid overload without benefit (WATERFALL 2022; ACG 2024); smaller volumes with heart failure or CKD.
No prophylactic antibiotics: antibiotics only for documented or strongly suspected infection (infected necrosis, cholangitis, other source) — ACG 2024; IAP/APA 2013.
Early oral feeding (within 24 h as tolerated); enteral rather than parenteral nutrition if oral intake fails.

[immediate] Suspected ectopic pregnancy seen in clinic (pain, bleeding or collapse with a positive pregnancy test): Outpatient clinic: obstetric emergency — call 911 or arrange immediate transfer to a hospital with an obstetric unit (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); inform the on-call obstetric team before arrival.
[immediate] Resuscitation: two large-bore IV cannulae; IV fluids; O2; crossmatch; urgent gynaecology review.
[surgical] Ruptured/haemodynamically unstable: emergency surgery — laparoscopy (salpingectomy), laparotomy if unstable; methotrexate and expectant management are contraindicated (NICE NG126).
[surgical] Unruptured ectopic with haemodynamic stability: laparoscopic salpingectomy (preferred) or salpingostomy (if contralateral tube damaged).

[conservative] Medical management with methotrexate (50 mg/m² IM, single dose) only for selected unruptured ectopics: haemodynamically stable, no significant pain, adnexal mass < 35 mm with no visible heartbeat, serum hCG < 1500 IU/L (may be offered up to 5000 IU/L), able to attend follow-up (NICE NG126).
[conservative] Expectant management only for clinically stable, pain-free women with a tubal ectopic < 35 mm, no visible heartbeat and serum hCG ≤ 1000 IU/L, with close follow-up (NICE NG126).

[followup] Serial β-hCG until negative when an unruptured ectopic was managed medically or expectantly (urine pregnancy test at 3 weeks after salpingectomy); anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU for rhesus-negative women having surgery for an ectopic pregnancy (NICE NG126).
Classic triad: amenorrhoea, lower abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding — but only 50% present classically.
Positive β-hCG with empty uterus on transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) = ectopic until proven otherwise.
Ruptured ectopic is a life-threatening emergency: shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation, haemodynamic collapse.
Ruptured or haemodynamically unstable ectopic: methotrexate and expectant management are contraindicated — emergency surgery (NICE NG126).

management.text: [immediate] Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.
[immediate] While waiting: two large-bore cannulae, bloods and crossmatch; alert the on-call vascular surgery team at the receiving hospital.
[conservative] Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics after blood cultures, per microbiology advice; prolonged antimicrobial therapy after graft infection (ESVS 2020).
[surgical] Vascular surgery: graft excision with in situ reconstruction or extra-anatomic bypass and repair of the bowel; endovascular stent-graft as a bridge in the unstable patient (ESVS 2020).
[followup] Lifelong vascular surveillance; long-term antimicrobial therapy as the vascular and infection teams advise (ESVS 2020).

Any gastrointestinal bleeding in a patient with an aortic graft (open repair or EVAR) is a secondary aorto-enteric fistula until proven otherwise; a self-limiting "herald" bleed often precedes exsanguinating haemorrhage (ESVS 2020).
CT angiography is the first test; endoscopy must not delay it, and a normal endoscopy does not exclude a fistula (ESVS 2020).

An obstructed, infected kidney is a urological emergency: urgent decompression (percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent) plus antibiotics; definitive stone treatment is delayed until the infection has resolved (EAU 2024).
Do not give medical expulsive therapy or attempt definitive stone treatment while infected.
Avoid NSAIDs in AKI, a solitary kidney or anuria.

• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics.

• IV Hartmann's 1L over 4h — ensure adequate hydration.
• Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance, urine output ≥ 0.5ml/kg/h.

management.text: Adhesive SBO — Failed Non-Operative Management
Surgery: laparoscopic (selected patients) or open adhesiolysis; assess bowel viability and resect non-viable bowel (WSES/Bologna 2017).
Do not repeat the contrast challenge.

- Insulin-treated diabetes: continue basal (long-acting) insulin — never omit it; give 80% of the usual dose the evening before and on the day; variable-rate IV insulin if more than one meal will be missed; capillary glucose and ketone monitoring; first on the list where possible (CPOC 2021).

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)

[surgical] Failure to resolve at 48–72 h, or ischaemia signs — emergency laparoscopy or laparotomy + adhesiolysis.
[surgical] Ischaemic bowel: resection ± primary anastomosis (Hartmann's if contaminated).
[followup] Counsel on recurrence risk (30% at 10 years); consider Seprafilm / icodextrin barrier at index surgery.

management.text: Small Bowel Obstruction — Non-Operative Trial
NGT on free drainage. IV fluid resuscitation. NBM. Serial clinical assessment every 4–6 h.
CT abdomen/pelvis to exclude closed-loop, ischaemia, or hernia.
Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) challenge: diagnostic and may be therapeutic; contrast not reaching the colon by 24 h predicts failure of non-operative management (WSES/Bologna 2017).
Failure criteria at 48–72 h: no resolution, worsening pain, peritonism, fever, rising lactate → operate.

[immediate] NG tube decompression; analgesia, antiemetics.

[conservative] SBO without strangulation (e.g. adhesions): non-operative management with NG decompression and IV fluids, plus a water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) challenge — contrast reaching the colon within 24 h predicts resolution (WSES 2017); if not resolved by 72 h, or any deterioration → laparotomy / laparoscopic adhesiolysis.

[conservative] Malignant obstruction (e.g. peritoneal carcinomatosis): MDT / palliative care discussion of goals of care; medical management (octreotide, hyoscine butylbromide, dexamethasone, venting gastrostomy) when surgery is not appropriate.
[followup] Elective laparoscopic adhesiolysis for recurrent adhesive obstruction.

management.text: Small Bowel Obstruction — Non-Operative Trial
NGT on free drainage. IV fluid resuscitation. NBM. Serial clinical assessment every 4–6 h.
CT abdomen/pelvis to exclude closed-loop, ischaemia, or hernia.
Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) challenge: diagnostic and may be therapeutic; contrast not reaching the colon by 24 h predicts failure of non-operative management (WSES/Bologna 2017).
Failure criteria at 48–72 h: no resolution, worsening pain, peritonism, fever, rising lactate → operate.

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)
[immediate] IV access, IV fluid resuscitation; correct electrolytes (potassium, magnesium); urinary catheter and fluid balance.
[immediate] NG tube decompression; analgesia, antiemetics.

[conservative] SBO without strangulation (e.g. adhesions): non-operative management with NG decompression and IV fluids, plus a water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) challenge — contrast reaching the colon within 24 h predicts resolution (WSES 2017); if not resolved by 72 h, or any deterioration → laparotomy / laparoscopic adhesiolysis.

[conservative] Malignant obstruction (e.g. peritoneal carcinomatosis): MDT / palliative care discussion of goals of care; medical management (octreotide, hyoscine butylbromide, dexamethasone, venting gastrostomy) when surgery is not appropriate.
[followup] Elective laparoscopic adhesiolysis for recurrent adhesive obstruction.

[surgical] Sigmoid volvulus — only if no peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation: endoscopic decompression (flexible sigmoidoscopy with a flatus / rectal tube), then sigmoid colectomy on the same admission if fit (ASCRS 2021). Ischaemia or perforation: emergency sigmoid resection.
[surgical] Caecal volvulus: endoscopic decompression is not recommended (avoid) — urgent right hemicolectomy / ileocaecal resection (ASCRS 2021).

[surgical] Left-sided malignant large bowel obstruction: resection or Hartmann's procedure, or a colonic stent (SEMS) as a bridge — stenting is contraindicated with perforation, impending caecal perforation, ischaemia or a closed loop (WSES 2018; ESGE 2020). Right-sided lesions: right hemicolectomy.

management.text: Colonic Volvulus (ASCRS 2021)
CT to confirm the site and look for ischaemia or perforation.

Sigmoid volvulus — only if no ischaemia, gangrene, perforation or peritonitis: endoscopic (flexible sigmoidoscopy) detorsion and decompression with a decompression tube; then sigmoid colectomy during the same admission if fit — recurrence is common.
Caecal volvulus: surgical resection — right hemicolectomy (primary anastomosis or ileostomy according to physiology); endoscopic detorsion is not recommended for caecal volvulus (avoid).
Peritonitis, gangrenous or perforated colon, or failed detorsion: emergency resection (sigmoid colectomy / Hartmann's procedure, or right hemicolectomy).

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after …(truncated)

- Emergency laparotomy / high-risk surgery: document the predicted mortality risk pre-operatively (NELA risk calculator or P-POSSUM); if ≥ 5%, consultant surgeon and anaesthetist present and planned post-operative critical care (NELA; RCS 2018 The Higher Risk General Surgical Patient). Age ≥ 65 or frail: elderly-medicine (geriatric) review.
[immediate] IV access, IV fluid resuscitation; correct electrolytes (potassium, magnesium); urinary catheter and fluid balance.
[immediate] NG tube decompression; analgesia, antiemetics.

[conservative] SBO without strangulation (e.g. adhesions): non-operative management with NG decompression and IV fluids, plus a water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) challenge — contrast reaching the colon within 24 h predicts resolution (WSES 2017); if not resolved by 72 h, or any deterioration → laparotomy / laparoscopic adhesiolysis.

[conservative] Malignant obstruction (e.g. peritoneal carcinomatosis): MDT / palliative care discussion of goals of care; medical management (octreotide, hyoscine butylbromide, dexamethasone, venting gastrostomy) when surgery is not appropriate.
[surgical] If strangulation, a closed loop, peritonism or a hernia is the cause: emergency laparotomy / laparoscopy; resect non-viable bowel.

[surgical] Sigmoid volvulus — only if no peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation: endoscopic decompression (flexible sigmoidoscopy with a flatus / rectal tube), then sigmoid colectomy on the same admission if fit (ASCRS 2021). Ischaemia or perforation: emergency sigmoid resection.
[surgical] Caecal volvulus: endoscopic decompression is not recommended (avoid) — urgent right hemicolectomy / ileocaecal resection (ASCRS 2021).

[surgical] Left-sided malignant large bowel obstruction: resection or Hartmann's procedure, or a colonic stent (SEMS) as a bridge — stenting is contraindicated with perforation, impending caecal perforation, ischaemia or a closed loop (WSES 2018; ESGE 2020). Right-sided lesions: right hemicolectomy.

Adhesions (60%) and hernias (20%) account for 80% of small bowel obstruction; in a virgin abdomen look for a hernia or tumour.

Non-operative management resolves most adhesive SBO without strangulation; a water-soluble contrast challenge predicts resolution (WSES 2017).

• Identify source of infection: CXR + urine dipstick + abdominal CT if no clear focus.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
INDICATIONS FOR SURGERY:
• Signs of bowel ischaemia (peritonism, lactate rising, pneumatosis on CT)
• Closed-loop obstruction on CT
• Complete SBO failing conservative management > 48h
• Strangulating hernia as cause

PRE-O …(truncated)
• Erect CXR — exclude free air and basal pneumonia.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Blood cultures × 2 before first antibiotic dose.
• Sepsis-6 bundle: O₂, cultures, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output monitoring, blood glucose.
• CT abdomen if abdominal source suspected — abscess, perforation, ischaemia.
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.
• Supplemental O₂: titrate to SpO₂ 94–98% (BTS 2017); reassess.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.

If suspected infection, sepsis bundle now: blood cultures and IV antibiotics within 1 h (SSC 2021).

Score action — NEWS2 14: High — NEWS2 >= 7: continuous monitoring and an emergency response by a team with critical-care skills; consider HDU/ICU. In the clinic, call 911 for transfer to the nearest emergency department (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 3: 2 or more — qSOFA >= 2: high risk of a poor outcome. If suspected infection, treat as sepsis: lactate, blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 h, fluid resuscitation guided by perfusion and senior review (SSC 2021); otherwise look for another cause of organ dysfunction.

management.text: - Beta-blocker (bisoprolol): tachycardia may be blunted — heart rate can under-read shock or sepsis (ATLS 10).

[immediate] Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.
[immediate] Direct admission to a hyperacute stroke unit / stroke team; nil by mouth until swallow screen.

[immediate] On a DOAC or warfarin: thrombolysis is usually contraindicated (stroke team decides on timing/levels); thrombectomy remains an option; intracerebral haemorrhage on an anticoagulant — urgent reversal.

[surgical] Ischaemic stroke: thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) within 4.5 h of onset if haemorrhage is excluded and no contraindication; mechanical thrombectomy for proximal anterior-circulation occlusion within 6 h (selected patients up to 24 h) — NICE NG128.

[conservative] Aspirin 300 mg once haemorrhage is excluded (if thrombolysed, from 24 h after it; thrombolysis is contraindicated on a DOAC unless the stroke team confirms it is safe); oxygen only if SpO₂ < 95%; swallow screen before oral intake.
[followup] Stroke rehabilitation; secondary prevention; defer elective surgery.

• Defer any elective surgery

• Urine ACR — hypertensive nephropathy screen.
• Document bilateral BP — coarctation exclusion if > 20mmHg differential.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common type (~80%); generally excellent prognosis with 10-year survival >95% for low-risk disease.
FNAC Bethesda V–VI confirms malignancy; molecular markers (BRAF, RAS) may aid indeterminate cases.

management.text: Non-Variceal Upper GI Bleed
PPI: esomeprazole 80 mg IV bolus then 8 mg/h infusion × 72 h (post-endoscopy high-risk lesion).
OGD within 24 h — endoscopic haemostasis (adrenaline injection + clip/bipolar coagulation) for active bleed or visible vessel.
H. pylori testing at endoscopy — eradication therapy if positive.

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Active bleeding / high bleeding risk: mechanical prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression) now; start LMWH once haemostasis is secure — reassess daily.

[immediate] Haematemesis, or melaena with shock or GBS ≥ 2, seen in clinic: Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.

[immediate] IV access × 2 large-bore; crystalloid resuscitation; restrictive red-cell transfusion — Hb threshold 70 g/L (target 70–90 g/L), 80 g/L (target ≥ 100 g/L) with cardiovascular disease (ESGE 2021); unstable patients to HDU/ICU (critical care).
[immediate] High-dose PPI before endoscopy may be considered; continue after endoscopic haemostasis of high-risk stigmata (ESGE 2021). No antifibrinolytic (HALT-IT 2020).
[immediate] Stop NSAIDs; review antithrombotics (see the patient-specific anticoagulant / antiplatelet advice).

[surgical] OGD within 24 h: peptic ulcer with high-risk stigmata — dual endoscopic therapy (adrenaline injection + clip or thermal coagulation). Suspected varices — variceal protocol (band ligation within 12 h).

[followup] H. pylori test-and-treat; PPI (8 weeks for ulcers); avoid NSAIDs long term; repeat OGD for gastric ulcers.

• Aspirin loading dose NOT suggested: aspirin/NSAID allergy or active bleeding recorded — discuss antiplatelet therapy with cardiology
• ST elevation / STEMI: immediate reperfusion — primary PCI pathway via cardiology (fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be delivered in time; ESC 2023)
• Oxygen only if SpO₂ < 90% (ESC 2023); IV access; continuous ECG monitoring during transfer
• Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital).
• Act on the critical result now: senior review, repeat and identify the cause

• Haemodynamically significant bleed: 2 × large-bore IV cannulae, crystalloid resuscitation, crossmatch; restrictive red-cell transfusion — threshold Hb 70 g/L (80 g/L with cardiovascular disease) (BSG 2019; NICE CG141).
• Urgent OGD / colonoscopy — within 24h of haemodynamic stabilisation.

• Consider anaphylaxis (IM adrenaline, RCUK 2021) and ruptured AAA (permissive hypotension, ESVS 2024) before fluids. Otherwise: 2 × large-bore IV cannulae, Hartmann's 500ml bolus — reassess BP and HR at 15 min.
• POCUS: cardiac (effusion/tamponade), aorta (AAA — bedside ultrasound of the aorta), IVC collapsibility.
• Contact appropriate specialty immediately: cardiology (MI/tamponade), surgery (haemorrhage/AAA), emergency medicine (PE).
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• GI scope (OGD + colonoscopy) — iron deficiency anaemia workup, exclude GI blood loss.
• Discuss transfusion threshold with patient (Hb < 8, symptomatic).
• Urine dipstick, urinalysis, albumin:creatinine ratio — AKI vs CKD differentiation.
• Hold NSAIDs, ACE-I, ARBs, metformin — nephrotoxic drugs peri-operatively.
• IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's) if pre-renal cause — reassess creatinine in 4–6h.
• Consider nephrology input if creatinine not improving after fluid resuscitation.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• IV fluid challenge 500ml if hypovolaemia likely — reassess HR at 30 min.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Hold NSAIDs 48h pre-operatively — renal protection.

Result action — Lactate 4.6 mmol/L: Lactate >= 4 mmol/L — Tissue hypoperfusion: find the cause (sepsis, bleeding, ischaemia, obstructive shock), resuscitate guided by perfusion, repeat lactate within 2-4 h, senior review and critical-care referral. If suspected infection, sepsis bundle now: blood cultures and IV antibiotics within 1 h (SSC 2021).

Score action — NEWS2 12: High — NEWS2 >= 7: continuous monitoring and an emergency response by a team with critical-care skills; consider HDU/ICU. In the clinic, call 911 for transfer to the nearest emergency department (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 3: 2 or more — qSOFA >= 2: high risk of a poor outcome. If suspected infection, treat as sepsis: lactate, blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 h, fluid resuscitation guided by perfusion and senior review (SSC 2021); otherwise look for another cause of organ dysfunction.

management.text: EMERGENCY — Variceal Upper GI Bleed (Baveno VII 2022)
Terlipressin 2 mg IV 4-hourly (or octreotide) as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected, for 2–5 days. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily prophylaxis for up to 7 days.
Restrictive red-cell transfusion: threshold Hb 70 g/L, target 70–80 g/L — avoid over-transfusion.
OGD within 12 h of presentation: endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL), or cyanoacrylate glue for gastric varices.

High risk of failure (Child-Pugh C 10–13, or B > 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy): pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h. Refractory bleeding: balloon tamponade or oesophageal stent as a bridge to rescue TIPS.

• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).
• Elective surgery deferred — INR must be < 1.5 pre-operatively.
• PO Vitamin K 1–2mg — slow INR correction (avoid over-reversal in warfarin patients).
• Repeat INR in 24–48h — confirm correction before rescheduling surgery.

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.

• Dietitian referral — pre-operative nutritional support. Delay elective surgery ≥ 4 weeks if possible.

management.text: EMERGENCY — Variceal Upper GI Bleed (Baveno VII 2022)
Terlipressin 2 mg IV 4-hourly (or octreotide) as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected, for 2–5 days. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily prophylaxis for up to 7 days.
Restrictive red-cell transfusion: threshold Hb 70 g/L, target 70–80 g/L — avoid over-transfusion.
OGD within 12 h of presentation: endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL), or cyanoacrylate glue for gastric varices.

High risk of failure (Child-Pugh C 10–13, or B > 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy): pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h. Refractory bleeding: balloon tamponade or oesophageal stent as a bridge to rescue TIPS.
- β-HCG: result required before surgery, ionising imaging or a drug that is unsafe in pregnancy — do not record it as negative without a result.

- VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89 2018): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery. Active bleeding / high bleeding risk: mechanical prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression) now; start LMWH once haemostasis is secure — reassess daily.

[immediate] Outpatient clinic: this is an emergency — call 911 for an ambulance or arrange immediate transfer to the nearest emergency department (OKEU Hospital, St Jude's Hospital or Tapion Hospital); start the first actions below while waiting and hand over in person.
[immediate] Two large-bore cannulae; cautious crystalloid resuscitation; restrictive transfusion — transfuse when Hb < 70 g/L to a target of 70–80 g/L (Baveno VII).
[immediate] Vasoactive drug as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected: terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 h until bleeding is controlled, then 1 mg every 4 h, for 2–5 days (Baveno VII / BSG 2015).
[immediate] Antibiotic prophylaxis: ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily for up to 7 days (Baveno VII).
[surgical] Endoscopy within 12 h: endoscopic band ligation (oesophageal varices); cyanoacrylate injection (gastric varices) — Baveno VII.
[surgical] High risk of failure (Child-Pugh C < 14, or Child-Pugh B > 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy): pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h (Baveno VII); refractory bleeding: rescue TIPS.
[followup] Secondary prophylaxis: non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol or carvedilol) plus band ligation programme; hepatology follow-up; alcohol cessation if relevant.

• Haemodynamically significant bleed: 2 × large-bore IV cannulae, crystalloid resuscitation, crossmatch; restrictive red-cell transfusion — threshold Hb 70 g/L (80 g/L with cardiovascular disease) (BSG 2019; NICE CG141).
• Urgent OGD / colonoscopy — within 24h of haemodynamic stabilisation.
• 12-lead ECG — pre-operative cardiac baseline (age ≥ 40).

• Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
• IV fluid challenge 500ml if hypovolaemia likely — reassess HR at 30 min.
• Urine protein:creatinine ratio — nephrotic syndrome (PCR > 300mg/mmol).
• Dietitian referral — pre-operative nutritional support. Delay elective surgery ≥ 4 weeks if possible.
• Prescribe ONS (Ensure/Fortisip) ×2 — pre-op nutritional optimisation (ERAS).
• If albumin < 25 g/L and surgery urgent: parenteral nutrition pre-operatively with nutrition team support.
Ask the question and record the answer under Medications → Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements
• Calculate FIB-4 score — non-invasive fibrosis assessment (cirrhosis risk).
Score action — NEWS2 3: Low — NEWS2 1-4: minimum 4-6-hourly observations; registered nurse assessment and decision on escalation (RCP NEWS2 2017).

Score action — qSOFA 0: Below 2 — qSOFA < 2 does not exclude sepsis: continue NEWS2 monitoring and reassess if infection is suspected (Sepsis-3; SSC 2021 advises against qSOFA alone as a screening tool).
